episodes.title: Creative Alchemy ep 14: Healing with Music During Cult Recovery weith Matthew Castle
episodes.description:
When Matthew Castle was 17 he took a small duffle bag and his violin and slipped out of a bedroom window of his family home. He was escaping a life in the high demand religion, the Institute of Basic Life Principles. Music had sustained him while he was growing up in IBLP and it would continue to do so once he was free and living an autonomous life.

In the introduction, I talk about how I could especially relate to part of Matthew's story where he talks about taking a break from the violin after he left IBLP. He wanted to see if his love for the violin was truly authentic and the way he found to do that was by taking a break from it. I went through a similar process post-cult where I examined many (many!) things in my life to determine if they were things I liked because liked them or because the cult told me I should like them.

I also talk about this week's Memoir Monday blog post where I explore the creative healing that can come from a psychological practise called Internal Family Systems (IFS). I will be doing a series of posts about IFS and creativity over the coming weeks.

- Growing up in Bill Gothard’s Institute of Basic Life Principles (IBLP)
- Questioning the blind obedience in IBLP
- Leaving home at age 17 through a bedroom window

- How music became the one thing Matthew felt accomplished at
- How music brings us into our bodies
- How music gave Matthew his life back
- Assisting husband Paul’s writing and illustrating children's books
- How music transcends language

episodes.title: The Healing Properties of Exposing Cult Secrets with Esther Friedman
episodes.description:
Secrets are toxic and damaging. If you’ve been in a cult you know this and you may also know how secrets can be used to control us when we’re in a high demand situation.




When today’s guest Esther Friedman left the cult she belonged to she took a very firm stance against secrets and I loved talking to her about this during our interview. I related to so much of what she had to say and since we spoke I’ve been reflecting on the destructive power of secrets.




In the introduction I talk about this conversation with Esther has had me reflecting on secrets and how cults use them. I was thinking about the concentric circles of secrets in the cult I belonged to. As a tactic for control and manipulation the cult leader I followed would keep secrets from the group and/or would let certain people know certain secrets and others in the group would be aware of this and know that they weren’t high enough in the group hierarchy to know those secrets.




In the sociological and psychological study of cults this is often called ‘information control’. Robert J. Lifton calls it ‘millieu control’. Steven Hassan talks about how cults teach different levels of information to different members of a group. Margaret Singer talks about how controlling information and keeping members unable to fully evaluate what is happening is central to coercive persuasion. 




So, secrets are a valuable tool to the cult leader. I experienced that and so did Esther. If you’ve been in a cult I think you’ll enjoy hearing about how Esther used creative expression to work through her feelings and process her anger after leaving ‘The School’.




I also reflect on the unexpected pleasure this podcast has brought me because it allows me to connect with other cult survivors. Interviewing my guests and talking about our shared experiences is healing something in me, and that’s not something I’d planned for with this show, but it’s a very welcome part of my experience. 





Esther Friedman is a licensed mental health counselor (LMHC), expressive art therapist, songwriter, recording artist, performer, and author of The Gentle Souls Revolution. This book depicts her 5-year misadventure in a “secret mystery school” that taught her how cults exploit human nature. She embraced her anger, formed a personal policy of No More Secrets, posted a blog, and started protecting her time and energy fiercely.  A funny thing happened: as she exposed cult secrets and reclaimed her voice, her heart calmed and her mind cleared. She took the narrative back, and her truth contradicted the group’s claimed ideology. Esther discovered that what was good for her was also good for the people that she loves. That’s the basis and therapy model for her clinical practice, The Gentle Souls Revolution.







Learn more about Ester Friedman at GentleSoulsRevolution.com





This episode of Creative Alchemy is supported by the audiobook version of my award-winning, Amazon best-selling memoir, Cult, A Love Story. 




Readers call the book ‘compelling’ ‘gritty’ ‘intimate’ and ‘not boring’ – which is what an author loves to hear. I narrated the audiobook and if you have a Spotify premium subscription you can listen to the audiobook for free as part of that subscription at alexandraamor.com/spotify.







You can listen above, on your favorite podcast app, or watch on YouTube. Notes, links, resources and a full transcript are below.




Show Notes




On being deliberately groomed and recruited into a secret cult



Leaving the group five years later and realizing how much secrecy was involved



The difference between secrecy and privacy



The cognitive load that secrets create



Reclaiming ownership of personal time



How expressing our feelings in writing can help us find our voice again



Only understanding what we’ve gone through when we write it down



How high-demand groups deliberately create confusion 



And how reverse engineering this confusion is healing



Reclaiming our identity in the cult recovery process



Knowing when to take a break from a writing project for self-care

Transcript of the interview with Esther Friedman



Alexandra: Esther Friedman, welcome to Creative Alchemy.




Esther: Thank you, Alexandra, for having me.




Alexandra: You’re so welcome. 




Please tell us a little bit about your background and also about the cult that you were involved in.



Esther: Well, maybe we’ll start with the cult. Because that led to the background, I guess. Although I had a master’s degree as an expressive arts therapist before the cult, but the cult is what led me to what I’m doing today. 




So the cult is something that you probably have not heard of because it’s very, very secretive. When I was in it, it was simply called School. It has also been called Odyssey Study Group. Back in the 60s and 70s, it was called the Theater of All Possibilities. But it was this very hush hush mom and pop. I sometimes jokingly call it cult light, but I think I just didn’t experience cult dark. 




It was philosophical, although it borrowed from the Bible, but I shouldn’t say borrowed. It stole from the Bible and New Age Oprah Winfrey type things, but really the main thing was a teaching called the Fourth Way, which started in the early 1900s with this George Ivanovich Gurdjieff that was kind of the main philosophical I guess underpinnings. 




Except that they never mentioned the Fourth Way or the man, they just trotted out the ideas. So I think I’m just giving you an example of how secretive the information was, the lack of transparency. But it was also the kind of thing where when you stumbled into this group and their recruitment process was-I’ll get-I’ll get into that if you want me to. 




It was very, very deceptive. That what you learn is like this is a secret, esoteric mystery school, and we considered ourselves to be the invisible world. It wasn’t like a living group, right? But we weren’t supposed to talk about it outside the group, which of course is a red flag-a screaming siren, right? So is that enough information about? 




Alexandra: How did you get involved, and what drew you to it? 



Esther: I like to say I wasn’t adulting well at that time in my life. I don’t know if you’re aware of Dan Shaw? He wrote the book Traumatic Narcissism. He’s a therapist in New York. He’s also a fellow survivor, but he has a formula that just fit my experience perfectly. It’s bad luck plus timing.




Things weren’t going well in my life. Like nothing was going well I was just at the tail end of a relationship. It was clear we were going to break up. I felt really lost with my career. I just felt like this adulting thing is just beyond me. I can’t figure it out. I feel like I don’t belong in the planet. 




So I’m feeling sorry for myself in line at Whole Foods, and a woman struck up a conversation with me. This is how the recruitment works for this school. It’s somebody just strikes up a conversation with you, and then foments. 




I use the word foment because it’s not nurturing; it fosters a friendship. So I spent a good couple of months with this woman, Lisa, calling me. Let’s get together. Let’s take a walk, and she was really nice and fun, and she would listen to me, and I was kind of yammering on and on about myself while she gathered the data. 




At the time, of course, I was pretty naive to all of this because she didn’t tell me much about herself at all. But I was yammering on and on. She gave me an opportunity because she wasn’t talking, and I was going on and on about how I can’t figure the world out. And so then after a couple of months, she said, “Oh, I want to introduce you to a friend.” 




She introduced me to Robert, who was really the leader of the group, but I didn’t find that out until I actually went to my first class and he pitched it as a five-week experiment. It sounded very innocuous.




The grooming begins in the friendship. At the time I’m looking for something and they’re like oh we offer these ideas and we help each other and Alexandra I honestly thought I was going to a potluck. I thought I was going to go to someone’s house, and there’d be a potluck, and we’d talk about ideas and laugh, and that it’d be really casual. And of course, it wasn’t that at all.




Alexandra: How long were you involved?



Esther: Five years.




Alexandra: And so, as you said, that led you to what you’re doing now, and I mentioned in my email that I sent you as we were setting up to do this interview, that I found this sentence on your website that just blew my socks off. So I want to read it for our listeners, and then we’ll talk about various pieces of it. 




You say, “I embraced my anger, formed a personal policy of no more secrets, posted a blog and started protecting my time and energy fiercely”, which I just love. I really want to delve into all of this. So the first thing you mentioned is that you embraced your anger. 




Why was that first on the list, and why was it so important?



Esther: I love this question because I think it’s important for every former cult member. I had spent five years increasingly losing any confidence. I didn’t have much confidence when I entered, right? And, of course, the first little bit is love bombing. But then, of course, that alternate starts alternating with the feeding frenzies, and of course, then the love bombing falls away, and you’re always getting hammered, right?

episodes.title: Creative Alchemy episode 12: Burning to Tell the Truth with Renee Linnell
episodes.description:
One of the big takeaways I have from this conversation with Renee Linnell was when she reminded me that shame dissipates as we tell our stories.

When we tell the truth about an experience we feel shame about, that act of speaking up breaks up the shame, the same way a frozen river’s ice breaks up in the spring. Telling the truth is like sunshine and warmth on that river of shame.

Even when we just tell the truth to ourselves. Perhaps especially then!

It’s hard to tell the truth sometimes. It can be scary and it can make us feel vulnerable. But it is always worth doing.

Renee talks about her journaling practice and how full of anger it was when she first left the cult. I’m glad we talked about that because expressing those feelings is SO important, especially after a cult situation where we’ve been told our thoughts and feelings and our very being don’t matter. It’s healthy to get the river of feelings flowing again.

Show Notes: 
- Knowing early on that a punishing deity didn’t make sense
- Starting a spiritual quest at age 15
- Creating the perfect life and still feeling empty and sad
- Falling under the spell of a toxic teacher
- Beginning to write as a way to deal with the difficult emotions after leaving a cult
- Finding that shame dissipates as we tell our stories
- Lessons learned about how to write a personal story
- Working with an editor and getting what was needed from that collaboration
- Moving through the painful process of working with edits
- Resisting suggestions to change the book for a publisher and telling the true story 
- How writing helps us to see our part in what unfolds in life
- Remembering the joy of creativity for its own sake

episodes.title: Writing About the Cult Next Door with Tamara Mathieu
episodes.description:
We all want to belong. As I’ve said previously on this show, we are wired to look for connection and community. That very natural human need is what led today’s guest, Tamara Mathieu, into the Twelve Tribes. Fourteen years later, Tamara and her husband realized they needed to leave what had become a controlling, high-demand situation. One that Tamara would end up writing a book about and telling the truth about her experience.




In the introduction, I talk about how personally satisfying for me to hear a cult-related story from someone who had got involved with her partner and then survived the cult with that person and then got out with him as well. And they’re still married now! I don’t know how many partnerships or marriages could survive that kind of journey.





Tamara Mathieu joined the Twelve Tribes religious cult in 2000, with her husband and young son. In her memoir, All Who Believed, she tells her story in depth from how she became drawn to the group, what the next fourteen years were like, and finally how her family left in 2014 as a family of six. Writing became a way for her to heal and share her experience in order to educate others about this insidious group.




Tamara lives in Vermont, works with adults with disabilities, and now has three grandchildren.







Learn more about Tamara Mathieu at TamaraMathieu.com

Show Notes




Searching for answers after the Columbine school shooting



On being introduced to the simple lives of those in the Twelve Tribes



Discovering that the reality was very different than the initial impression of the group

Transcript of the interview with Tamara Mathieu



Alexandra: Tamara Matthew, welcome to Creative Alchemy.




Tamara: Hi, thank you for having me.




Alexandra: My pleasure. 




Tell us a little bit about yourself and about your background in the Twelve Tribes.



Tamara: I live in Swanton, Vermont. I am a mother of four children. I now have three granddaughters as well. I grew up in Vermont, and I met my husband in 1995. We were both UVM students, University of Vermont, and around let’s see, it must have been 1998. 




I found out that I was pregnant, and so our lives just took a very different turn. We were still in college and everything, and now we have a baby on the way. And I took that responsibility very seriously that I was going to be a mother. 




We bought a house, we planned a wedding, and I really started to consider being a mother. What kind of mother was I going to be? I wanted to be a good mother. I really wanted a secure and stable family for my child. You know, all those things. Once my baby was born, I remember an event that really just is in my mind, as one of those moments that I feel like I started searching for something more was when the Columbine shooting happened. 




My baby Emmett was only five weeks old, and I was very affected by that event. Now that I would potentially be sending my child to school in a few years, and that was so scary. And I thought, am I going to be able to do that? Am I going to feel safe? Is this going to get worse? Is this kind of thing going to be happening more and more? 




It just was very unsettling, very scary, and I really started at that point to just desire just something safe, something different, something secure, just something wholesome for my child. I was a stay-at-home mom at the time, and I had mom friends, and we had play group. I had a good support in that way, but still, the majority of my day of my time was just me alone in our home with my baby. That was just awfully lonely considering that I was 22 years old and I went from college student. 




We lived in an apartment with like seven of our friends. There was always something going on, and just carefree and fun. And then all of a sudden, I had this drastic, drastic life change. And I think it’s often in those times where anybody could be susceptible to the message of a group such as the Twelve Tribes, because it was kind of in this state of mind that I met the Twelve Tribes.




I was so drawn to their simple life of being together. From the outside, the appeal was so strong. I just saw families living together, working together, mothers helping each other out-a really simple and wholesome lifestyle that I felt like I would not, in and of myself, be able to provide for my child. Like, how am I going to have this simple farm lifestyle? 




We lived in Burlington, Vermont. My husband was a software engineer. Everything in our lives was kind of driving us to a certain lifestyle, which would have been probably most young women’s dream. We probably would have ended up fairly wealthy with my husband getting into that field in the late ’90s. It was a really upcoming field. He already had a really good job. We were homeowners at 22 years old; that’s unheard of. It was in that place that I was lonely and just looking for something more. 




I will back up a little bit. My husband’s aunt, his mother’s sister, joined the Twelve Tribes way back in its beginnings in Island Pond, Vermont, in 1981. He grew up always knowing about the group. His family lived in Benson, Vermont. He’d been up to Island Pond to visit his relatives, and so I was introduced to the group through him, meeting his relatives.




What really stood out to me, I’d met some people in the community prior to our wedding, but the day of our wedding, he had relatives that came up. Twelve Tribes don’t go into churches, and they don’t go to ceremonies such as weddings, so they came to the reception afterwards, and they just pitched in. We didn’t have fancy caterers or anything like that. It was just all hands on deck. And so they just saw that there was a need, and they pitched in and they started replenishing food at our buffet and making sure everybody had water. 




And they stayed afterwards, and they cleaned our entire reception hall. We were expecting to have to go back and do that basically ourselves. And we show up, and there they are, and they’re cleaning. I was really affected. It’s like, wow, this is amazing. These people are so wonderful. They don’t even know me, and their work. It was a really hot day, and one of them had a baby in a front carrier. 




And then the next day, a whole bunch of Twelve Tribes members came over to my in-laws’ house. There’s a community in Rutland, Vermont, which is nearby, and a bunch of people from there came over. I was just surrounded by probably four to five different Twelve Tribes families, and I just spent hours asking them questions and talking to them. There were a couple of other young women that also had babies, and I just remember being envious of them. They’re all going home to this wonderful life together. And the next day, I had to just go back to Burlington to our lonely house. And my husband was going back to work.




We had a three month old baby. He had just started a job at a new company, so we weren’t going on a honeymoon. It was just like okay, I just met this amazing group of people. I want to find out more. I want to get to know them more. So I started visiting any chance I could get. I went with my mother and father-in-law to Hyannis, Massachusetts, for a whole week. My husband didn’t go, but you know he felt fine sending me and our baby with his parents to visit the Twelve Tribes. No harm was going to come out of that. 




But the more time I spent there, it was harder and harder for me to go home. I started reading all of their literature. And my mother-in-law would get that they have like a monthly newsletter for the group. It’s called the Intertribal News, and every single Twelve Tribes community around the world each month submits like just a little synopsis. Here’s what’s going on in our clan this month. Because she was good friends with a lot of the people in the Rutland location, she became privy to they would let her take and read these newsletters. She would give them to me, and I’d be so excited to read it, and my husband was not excited at first. About the thought of the Twelve Tribes. 




He was happy with our life, and he was raised Christian, and he really wanted me to be a Christian. This is another aspect of it. He wanted me to go to church with his family, and I was never drawn to religion at all. I had all these questions; it never made sense to me, and I felt like, well if if there was something that was the truth, and God wanted me to believe that, then, like surely I would have some type of internal response when I did finally find what I was looking for, and I felt like that’s what had happened. I never went to church and had that sense of like, oh my god, I can’t wait. Next Sunday, you know that was a great sermon. It was amazing. Can’t wait to go back.

episodes.title: Creative Alchemy episode 10: From Experience to Stories to Stage with Dennis Hawkins-Bogle
episodes.description:
Here’s what I was reminded of during this conversation with writer and playwright Dennis Hawkins-Bogle. No one’s going to hand you the opportunity to tell the truth of your experience and tell your story. There is no validation and acknowledgement fairy who’s going to come along and anoint you with her magic wand. If telling your story matters enough to you - if you feel the pull to tell the truth about your experience, whatever it is - you are going to have to be the one that makes it happen. And here’s the good news: it is within your power to do so.

In the introduction, I talk about my experience of watching Dennis perform his play, The Blue Taffeta Party Dress, and how I was struck by his ease and comfort on the stage, and both the joy and poignance I experienced while watching it.

- How writing and performing can bring new layers of understanding to an experience
- Telling stories that involve other people and being respectful while also telling the truth
- Writing prose vs. writing for the stage
- Memorizing 8,800 words to be performed

episodes.title: Writing to Reckon with a Cult Experience with Gerette Buglion
episodes.description: When we leave a high demand group, there is a reckoning that needs to happen. As survivors, we need to come to terms with so many things; among them, why we were drawn into the group in the first place and how we were affected by that situation. We need to deal with feelings that might include grief and loss and trauma and guilt. There's so much to unpack! My guest today, Gerette Buglion, understands this intimately. She herself is a cult survivor. And she hosts a writing program called Writing to Reckon which is specifically for cult survivors. In the introduction, I talk about the phenomenon of scapegoating that happens in cults. In the interview, Gerette mentions her own experience of being labelled a 'loser' by the leader of the cult she was involved in and I reflect on my personal experience with similar treatment of myself and others in the cult I belonged to. I also talk about how complicated it is to unpack these traumatic experiences that happen to us in cults. Gerette Buglion wants to live in a world where cult leaders, narcissistic abusers, and unethical, manipulative techniques are spotted, called out, and silenced, creating more opportunities for nourishing relationships to flourish. She is the author of two books: her memoir, An Everyday Cult, and the Writing to Reckon Journal – for Survivors of Spiritual, Religious, and Cultic Abuse. Her work as educator and consultant centers on liberation from coercive control and supporting the integrative power of writing for survivors of cultic relationships through Writing to ReckonTM programs and Reclaiming Autonomy Through the Written Word – a bi-annual writing symposium for survivors. She is Co-founder and Executive Director for the nonprofit Living Cult Free. You can learn more about Gerette Buglion at GeretteBuglion.com This episode of Creative Alchemy is supported by the audiobook version of my award-winning, Amazon best-selling memoir, Cult, A Love Story. I narrated the audiobook and if you have a Spotify premium subscription you can listen to the audiobook for free as part of that subscription at alexandraamor.com/spotify . Gerette: I am so glad to be here. What a pleasure! Alexandra: It's great to see you. Tell us a little bit about your background and about the cult that you were involved with. Gerette: I was born into a large family and grew up in a, I would say, a normally dysfunctional family. Nothing, you know, dramatic there, and I grew up in New York State of the United States, and when I was in my 30s, I got involved with a group that was centered on working with dreams. I had been interested in dreams, and I had a couple colleagues. I taught in a Waldorf school, so I had kind of a spiritually oriented bent much of my adult life, and a couple of my colleagues were doing this work, and so I got excited, and I got involved. At first, it was really lovely. I learned a lot. It was an opportunity for inner growth. And then over the years, I was involved for 18 years altogether. My daughter was born six months before I started. I had been interested in starting working with this teacher. I call him Doug in my book. I had been interested in working with Doug actually before before my daughter was born, but I put that off a bit because I felt it wasn't good to start something new when I was you know preparing to welcome a child into the world, my first child. There was a lot of anticipation in working with him too. But the first five years, I think, was fairly light involvement, and then that grew gradually over the years, as I became more and more, as the work we called it, became more and more a central focus in my life, and as my children grew. I bought a business based on my ex teacher's advice. Of course, he had no training in business consultation, nor did he have a marriage and family counseling license, but I also did couples work with him. My husband was also in the same group. He was involved for 16 years, and he left actually while doing his training to become a licensed clinical mental health counselor. That was part of his waking up to the fact that this was not a cool thing to be doing, because some of his professors started pushing him a bit. He had a few experiences with Doug that were really questionable and made him think again, and so he left, and then that gave me an opportunity to go even deeper. So my last two years in the cult were actually the most intense for me, and even the few years before that had been kind of growing in intensity. Do you want me to just share briefly how I left? There was a crisis in the organization, and that crisis was that six of the head teachers left on the very same day. That was like this earthquake, it was a massive, massive rupture. I had this question, this burning question of like, why would they all leave on the same day? Because so much of what this group was about in terms of personal growth was that we got to make choices based on what was being revealed to us through our individual dreams. So it was one thing for one teacher to say, “Hey, I'm I'm done”. That would be a hard thing, but totally acceptable. And in fact, that's something that would happen. People would come to a place that they're like I'm done, but then they would often come back. That actually is something that I did a couple of times. So we had this appearance of autonomy and choice being stitched into this organization, but it was really a ruse. And so, when all six of the top teachers left on the same day, there was a major, you know, WTF. What is really going on here? That led me to have an experience in a final meeting that we had with those teachers. One of them, literally in the last five minutes of our meeting, shared things, shared how she was being verbally beaten down by our teacher, and so that's what created the cognitive dissonance in me. It's like, wait a minute, this man that I've put on a pedestal is doing that to this beloved person who I know, who's an artist and a poet and a deeply sensitive person. It was really that cognitive dissonance that made the opening, that was the crack, that really allowed me to free myself. I had a very sudden snapping. I call it my snapping out of the cult, and my husband was really waiting for me. He had recognized that if he started pushing me in those two years to come out, that I would have left him. And I would have, because I was so completely indoctrinated at that point. So he really held the space for me, welcomed me back, as did many of my friends who had watched me kind of disappear for 18 years into this group. Alexandra: You mentioned your book there, which is called An Everyday Cult. Once this happened and you decided to leave, how did you use writing to help you with that part of the journey? Gerette: I love that question because writing is a huge part of my life. As I mentioned, I had good friends who really welcomed me back with open arms. One of them handed me an eight CD pack of Dr. Dan Siegel's interpersonal neurobiology. Have you ever heard of Dr. Siegel? Oh gosh, I cannot recommend his work highly enough because it was deeply important for me. Because there are many things he focuses on, as I said, interpersonal neurobiologists. He's a psychologist who has a neurological understanding and also a deeply relational understanding of the human experience. I listened to one of those CDs probably a dozen times, and the one that I listened to again and again, and this was in 2014 is when I left the group. The one I listened to focused on what Dr. Siegel calls the importance of creating a “coherent narrative out of traumatic or confusing experiences”. That was like gongs going off for me. I have always been an educator. I was a teacher of elementary students, and also did parent education. And I had even, as I was a special educator, so I had an orientation towards brain development and healthy human development. So hearing Dr. Siegel's work was very impactful for me, and so the coherent narrative became like this. It's hard to describe it, Alexandra. It almost was like a guiding impulse in my psyche. I felt like one of those homing pigeons. Wherever I was able to to actually speak to people in a safe space, that was part of creating a coherent narrative. I had also been a journaler my whole life, and there was an aberration of journaling that took place in the group, where we had to write about our pathology is what we called it, and the deep delving of how how broken we were, and how the guidance of our teacher was setting us free. So that was part of what was actually required. When I started writing for myself, there was this powerful reclamation of my own voice, because in the cult, I was one of the members of the group that was always the loser. I was one of the ones that was just never going to get it. There were others who would go up the ladder pretty quickly in understanding, and I might take a few steps forward, but then there'd be a slide back. That was my trajectory was a pretty rocky one. So to actually recognize that there was something of value, not only for myself, but also even for one or two other people, the writing just became this pathway, this doorway to finding, refinding my own voice and what I thought, how I think, what matters to me. Alexandra: So this idea of coherent narrative-you said that was kind of a homing beacon for you. Were you writing to find that coherent narrative? Is that the right way to describe it? Gerette: There was, and continues to be a continual kind of opening that takes place. The written word is leading me to deeper and richer, more nuanced, and more relational richer, actually, understanding of not only myself but also of the world. So, yeah, I think that the writing just kept opening, kept, and continues to open these these doors. Does that answer your question? Alexandra: It does. I'm just not understanding the connection between Dr. Siegel's work and writing. Gerette: The coherent narrative is where it actually intersects with therapy, with healing through therapy. So, when I was immersed in the cult, I believed that I understood who I was and what was most important, and how I could learn and grow, and what my role was in the world. But that was my cult identity that had actually been formed by my ex teacher. He harnessed my dreams, and harvested various images and experiences from my dreams to get me to believe that I was someone who was other than who I was. I believed, like I said, I was a loser. I was someone who was so damaged and so filled with pride, that was part of my cult identity persona. So that pride was something that he would continually berate me for. That I needed to become a humble servant of the animus in dream language. To have the experience of recognizing how detrimental that was, and how opposed to my true self Doug's narrative was, leaves me with a well, then, who the heck am I? The coherent narrative is an opportunity to tug at those strings and bring those questions and hold them long enough to discover what words might actually emerge, and the words that emerged … some of them were very confused. There's no question. I mean, you've written a book too, you know. Like there are, there were swaths of my writing that when I was editing, I would go back into and say, “What the heck is that? But that, that, that writing process was part of finding the coherence. Alexandra: Got it. That's yeah. I get it now. Thank you. Gerette: Thanks for the question. Alexandra: When did it occur to you that you might want to write a book about this experience? Gerette: I was about five years out of the cult, and I was sitting with a new friend and colleague, who was a writing coach. We were actually in a business group together, and just having a coffee chat, and she like just implored me to write. I was like, I don't know. I was really uncertain at first. We actually started a process together where she assured me that she would be able to support me in that process. She also had had her own experience of cultic involvement, so that being seen in that way was very important for me, and that was a big part of what helped me to realize the value of writing. When I first started writing, I'm a diehard educator, so I wanted to write something that was going to help people. So I was writing. I was actually with her when we were talking about genre and stuff, and to realize that I was starting to write a self-help book, and I was like, “Oh no, that's not what I want to be doing.” Because the cult that I was in was part of the self help movement, self help world. I worked for a couple years on it in that way, and I was struggling to find my voice because I could feel like even in terms of what tense to use and how to form these questions and responses. One day, I was sitting with a fellow cult survivor, I call him a cult buddy. So I was sitting with him, kind of angsting about it, and he looked at me and he's like, “Gerrette, what if you just wrote your story?” Again, that was just like gongs, and then that was the turning for me. Then it was relatively easy, because then it wasn't like I was trying to convince anybody of anything, or show that I was smart or had something of value. It's like, oh, actually, this is what happened to me. And as far as that coherent narrative goes, that's where things really started to crystallize because I saw the different phases of the cultic involvement that I had experienced. Of course, my experience was going in as an adult, rather than someone who was born in, and so to reckon with those choices that I had made as an educated, caring woman in my small community here. There was a lot of reckoning to do there, and what emerged was a deeper and richer understanding of the forces of indoctrination and the mechanisms of control, and of course that combined with I was very fortunate to find a good therapist within a year of leaving, and that helped me dramatically. I was also able to kind of weave that work into my book as well. Alexandra: You've touched on something that's always really fascinating for me. When I wrote my book, I learned a lot about the cult. I started writing it eight years after, and the way that I say it is by having to sort of go up to 30,000 feet and explain it to people so that they would understand, I learned a lot about what was going on with the manipulation by the cult leader. Was there anything that came out of your writing your book that was like that? Gerette: Oh, absolutely! Yeah, understanding dreams as something that is so deeply personal, and how a dream, they're ours, you know. We have them at night. They come to us. They don't belong to anybody. But how a dream could be manipulated. That mechanism of the twisting of meaning, which is something that I see living in the United States, I see that in a deeply disturbing way in the in the current administration. I was actually writing my book during the first term of his administration, and Alexandra, I actually had the naive belief at that time that, oh, this is so great! People will see on such a big scale how narrative can be twisted. We get to recognize this. We get to see it. We get to wake up to it, and we get to say no to it. I wrote one of my early blog posts was “Thank you, Donald.” Well, that was my own naivete, obviously, and yet there's something there. There's something about the recognition of how something of value, something of integrity, can be turned against us individually, and can be turned against us on a societal level. So there's definitely a profound, I would say, interweaving today of what I have come to terms with in my own lived experience, and how that manifests today in the wider societal authoritarianism that is ravaging our dear planet. Alexandra: What challenges did you experience writing this book? You've talked about one already about how you had a little bit of trouble finding your voice. Was there anything else you encountered that was challenging? Gerette: One thing that just pops up when you ask that question is the publishing process. I worked with a hybrid publisher. It was very thrilling and empowering for me to be accepted by this small hybrid press that doesn't publish everything. They decide what they want to publish, and so it was affirming. It was really empowering to have them choose my pitch, and bigan to work with them. There was a point in that process close to the end where we're finalizing things like book cover and design, and those final details, the blurbs on the front and back, and all of that kind of stuff, and there was something really wrong with the art that was used for. It was actually the photography of the art that I had. I actually had someone design the art for it. When I brought that to the attention of the publisher, they pushed back, or this one person in particular pushed back really hard, and started bullying me, and really like it was actually a recreation of the kinds of language that I experienced in the cult, and that was deeply destabilizing. It took me a little while to realize what was going on. It also was an opportunity for me to see it. Name it, and say actually, it's not going to happen that way. We are going to rephotograph the artwork because the color and the quality is terrible in what you're proposing to use. It's not right. I held my own, and that process was actually really affirming. So that's an example of a major challenge that ended up positive. There's, I mean, there's the process of promoting the book. I'd say that is oh, isn't that fun? That's a challenge. I discovered that I actually really love doing readings, but scheduling the readings and the organizational stuff I find challenging. Those are a few things that come to mind, anyway. I'm sure that there's definitely more. Alexandra: Those are some great examples. What advice can you offer to those who are thinking about writing a book about a cult experience or a traumatic experience, about where they can begin, because you work with writers. Where do you recommend someone start? Gerette: It's so individual, isn't it? Because we all have our unique triggers, and we all have our unique openings. I think learning enough about oneself is most important. I highly recommend finding a good therapist, someone who really understands coercive control. I know people who have been in therapy for years and years, but they don't know the coercive control piece. And I feel like there's still some arrested development where in a cultic environment, our development gets stopped. So having a therapist who really understands trauma and really understands the mechanisms of coercion can be incredibly helpful. As a starting place, I would definitely recommend that. The other piece that is really big for me is understanding how cultic trauma is ultimately relational trauma, and so finding environments where there can be some relational healing is also very important. I didn't know when I started Writing to Reckon, the classes and workshops that I offer, I didn't know that that's what I was offering.But over the years that has become more and more clear to me that what takes place in a small group where there is an understanding that everyone there has experienced some version of coercion or manipulation, or cultic abuse, or religious trauma. There's enough of a container that people get to find their own words and dare to share them with each other, and through that process, there is just this incredibly life affirming, like if I can use the word soul, soul growing experience in the personality. The whole being of the person gets to heal when you're seen by people who get it, people who you don't have to explain yourself to. There's there's an understanding there. It's an incredibly beautiful experience that I have the privilege of experiencing every Friday in the Writing to Reckon class, and then whenever I do workshops. I'm not saying that you have to come to a Writing to Reckon class, although of course anybody is welcome to. It's more finding the places where you can exercise that atrophied muscle of being in relationship with others. We're a social species. We need each other to grow, to be the most human we can be. We need each other. We can't do it in isolation. Alexandra: You mentioned your Writing to Reckon classes. What does reckoning mean to you and to your students? Gerette: I love that question. Reckoning is an opportunity to get really honest with what is, what happened, what exists in the moment, and in a certain way, to hit the pause button on all the ideas that our brain, or the internet, or all of the books that we read, or our therapist, even or our family and friends, or even our most trusted ones. It's like putting a pause on all of that noise and just saying, “Okay, I see this moment. This moment.” What I'm talking about here, Alexandra, is that we work with a writing prompt, and that prompt. I mean, you don't have to work with prompt. There's no requirements at all. But we come together around a certain concept. For example, I'm a nerdy educator, and it might be. So I've got all these people. I love the work of Daniel Kenneman, the book Thinking Fast and Slow. I love the work of Robert Chaldini, influence. Robert J. Lifton is my hero, who I came close to meeting, but unfortunately didn't. So, I might take a little snippet of one of their concepts, and then bring it into something that's happening in the world today that reminds me of the cultic experience. It's like there's a little nugget that we kind of plonk in front of us for a moment, and then we see where that takes us. The opportunity of just trusting the words that come, and then having the next opportunity of sharing those words and hearing ourselves speak them out loud by reading our writing, reading what we. Even the next step of actually hearing others who just heard our writing offer their feedback about what they loved, that's what reckoning is. It's like we're taking a lived experience, exploring it, and also getting some feedback on it. There is a kind of alchemy, actually, that happens in that experience that just allows us to become more autonomous through that process. I watch people become better writers through this really simple process. I watch people grow and integrate, and their voices strengthen. And you've experienced this too, I'm sure. Like it's just an exquisite experience, Alexandra: Something that comes up a lot on this podcast about creating and using creativity as a part of the healing process after a cult experience is how powerful telling the truth is. It sounds like reckoning in your definition is really telling the truth. That is built in there as well, and people have the experience of telling their own truth and finding their voice in that, and then getting positive feedback about it from others. Gerette: Absolutely, absolutely. It's just that this is what happened. There's something about the reckoning process that encourages us to strip away all those narratives of justification that we may have built in to just allow ourselves to kind of sleep at night. When we strip away those justifications or the narratives that other people had told us, or their explanations, or whatever, not only do we get to sleep better at night, we actually get to stand up a little taller, because we know who we are in an unfiltered way, and it's amazing. Alexandra: Oh, that's so lovely. Another part of your work is the Living Cult Free project. Tell us about that. Gerette: Oh, great! Living Cult Free is a nonprofit dedicated to exactly that, to cult-free living, and specifically in finding supporting individuals through education and empowering them to autonomous living in whatever ways. We're a small nonprofit and we have big hopes and are working towards really growing more and more. One of the ways that we're growing right now is actually through our partnership with a project that I started in September of 2024, which is offering a writing symposium. The writing symposiums bring speakers, all of whom are survivors and authors and writers in a variety of ways, meaning memoir writers, screenwriting, even graphic novelists come. So there's a wide variety of of writing. Creative expression through the written word in all of its manifestations. Living Cult Free has a scholarship fund, and so people get to attend the the symposium, the writing symposium. The name of that symposium is “Reclaiming Autonomy Through the Written Word for survivors of spiritual, religious, and cultic abuse”. Because of this beautiful partnership with Living Cult Free, we're able to offer scholarships for those who would otherwise be unable to attend. Scholarships have also been given to attend other educational resources so people can apply to receive a scholarship. It's a beautiful organization that is dedicated to growing slowly and organically, because of the dangers inherent in creating an organization. You laugh. Do you know anything about that? Alexandra: Maybe something. Yeah. Gerette: Exactly. We've been through a lot since the organization began back in 2020, but we feel there's a wonderful board of directors. People can look at the Living Cult Free website and sign up to be on the newsletter. What I should say is that that newsletter is twice a year. If people are interested in a more substantial newsletter, I do send out a weekly newsletter that is educationally oriented. So my nerdy educator self gets to play every week, and for me that's one of the ways that I get to keep growing. I know that I went on three different tangents there, but I hope that's all okay. I hope it made sense. Alexandra: Tell us where we can find more about Living Cult Free. Gerette: Living Cult Free can be found at livingcultfree.org. Alexandra: Perfect. And then the symposium. Tell us more about that. Gerette: Reclaiming Autonomy Through the Written Word. We actually have one that's coming up really soon. October 3 is the next one. The symposiums happen twice a year, and this symposium is featuring three different speakers. One is Dr. Laura Anderson, who is the founder of the Center for Trauma and Recovery Resolution, and she's also the author of When Religion Hurts. Do you know that book? Alexandra: That rings a bell with me. Gerette: It's a wonderful book. She is just an absolute fount of passion and education for survivors of coercion, especially those who have experienced religious trauma. I'm thrilled to have Dr. Laura Anderson speaking. I also have Robin Boyle Lazier, who is a legal scholar who just wrote a book on the title is “Taken No More: Protect Your Children Against Traffickers and Cults”, and she has worked for many years with ICSA, the International Cultic Studies Association, and she's on the board of ICSA. Robin has been a colleague for a number of years, and I am thrilled beyond measure to have her as a speaker. Also, and the third speaker is Hoyt Richards, who is a one of the founding board members of Living Cult Free, and he is also a featured in an HBO documentary that just came out. I don't know if you can get that documentary in Canada yet. I know a Canadian friend who found it somewhere, but it's called “Bring Me the Beauties”. It's a really interesting three-part docu-series. And it's actually just-I don't know what it is right now-but a couple weeks ago, it was rated as HBO's top documentary. It features his story, and Hoyt, what's unique about him is that while he was immersed in a new agey spiritual cult, he was also a rising star in the modeling industry. He became one of the very first male supermodels. That was happening while he was in the cult. It's a very interesting story, and the real story is the human story of what has taken place since he left, how he has healed with his family, and how he is growing individually. So, to have Hoyt be a speaker, he is also a screenwriter, and has written a number of films, so he will be speaking more from the screenwriting perspective. So I'm thrilled to have him at the symposium as well. Alexandra: Is there a website for the symposium? Gerette: You would just go to my website, which is gerretbuglion.com, and click on symposium, and all the information is there. Alexandra: Okay, perfect. That's a great segue into you telling us where we can find out more about you and your work. Gerette: Well, that's the spot, gerettebuglion.com.You can contact me, sign up for my newsletter. I am always happy to do what I call a 20 minute chat. You can schedule that any time because I'm always happy to not only just connect with fellow survivors, but also see if I can offer resources for people in whatever way that might be a good fit. Then also to see if any of my services, the writing support that I offer, might be a good fit or not. I want to also mention that the symposium, I really try to keep it affordable for people, and it's $39 for this three hour symposium that's very rich in content. Like I mentioned, people can apply for scholarship funds too, and I do pay my speakers. That's part of why that's part of why I charge for it because and that's really important to me because I value the time. So many of us were abused through volunteerism in our various cultic experiences. So I do pay my speakers as well as possible. Alexandra: Oh, that's amazing! Well, thank you, Gerette. I'm going to put links in the show notes to all those things so that people can find them going forward. Thank you so much for being with me. This has been a really rich conversation. I've really enjoyed it. Gerette: Yes, it's been my pleasure. Absolutely, thank you so much. Alexandra: You're so welcome. Take care. Bye Click here to grab your complimentary copy of the Creative Alchemy journaling handbook.
