episodes.title: Disentangling Religion from Personal Spirituality with Kimber Young
episodes.description: Kimber Young can trace her Mormon family lineage directly back to Brigham Young, the second president of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints. The Mormon church, she points out, was her whole life and her whole family was involved. And yet, somehow, Kimber was able to begin questioning the church doctrine and dogma while also retaining a sense of her own spirituality, which was so important to her. For anyone who's ever left a high demand situation, you know that this is an extremely difficult needle to thread. It is one I was particularly interested to talk to her about. In the introduction I talk about my experience with how challenging it is to question a group or religion that we've become bonded to (or, in Kimber's case, were born into), partly because this questioning is so threatening to our identity. Who are we without the group? It takes courage to ask that kind of question and the other questions that arise when we're challenging our beliefs. Kimber Young is an artist, writer, and creator of Something for Sundays, a weekly Substack newsletter and a monthly illustrated zine exploring religion, spirituality, meaning, and the big questions of being human. After growing up in a religious tradition and spending years questioning and reconstructing her beliefs, Kimber became fascinated by the ways people across cultures make meaning, practice spirituality, and understand the world around them. Her work is an invitation to stay curious, and build a spiritual life outside of the box. Learn more about Kimber Young at SomethingForSundays.Substack.com This episode of Creative Alchemy is supported by the audiobook version of my award-winning, Amazon best-selling memoir, Cult, A Love Story. Readers call the book 'compelling' 'gritty' 'intimate' and 'not boring' – which is what an author loves to hear. I narrated the audiobook and if you have a Spotify premium subscription you can listen to the audiobook for free as part of that subscription at alexandraamor.com/spotify . You can listen above, on your favorite podcast app , or watch on YouTube . Notes, links, resources and a full transcript are below. Show Notes Growing up in the Mormon church Some of the benefits of belonging to a tightly knit religious or spiritual organization How and when Kimber's questioning of the church began Navigating asking questions of a high-demand religion without giving up God How questioning a religion or spiritual group can threaten the parts of ourselves that we like Processing and disentangling through writing How posting writing publicly opened up conversations with family and friends Dealing with pushback about public posts Exploring other religions to see what might fit How audacity is more important for artists than talent Becoming comfortable with the mysteries of life and not knowing the answers How writing can help us to learn to think critically Resources mentioned in this episode Kimber's Substack, Something for Sundays Kimber's post Done, Not Perfect East of Eden by John Steinbeck The Artist's Way by Julia Cameron Combatting Cult Mind Control by Steve Hassan We don't discuss it during the interview, but one of my favourite books about someone wrestling with the Mormon religion is Leaving the Saints by Martha Beck Transcript of the interview with Kimber Young Alexandra: Kimber Young, welcome to Creative Alchemy. Kimber: Thank you for having me. I'm so excited to be here. Alexandra: I'm so glad that you agreed to come and talk to me. Give us a little bit about your background as we begin. Kimber: I was actually born in Oregon, but mostly raised in Utah, and I grew up as a member of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, which is the official name, but colloquially known as Mormons. My background really is about that because it just informed every aspect of my life, and I come from Latter Day Saint descent on both sides. My great great great great uncle is Brigham Young, who brought all the people over to Utah, so it's very ingrained into our family culture and identity, and my identity as well. And when I think about my upbringing, it really is a lot Mormonism. Alexandra: I was just reading a post. I had a few minutes to kill before we started, and I was reading a post that you wrote recently on Substack, and you were talking about how devoted you really were. Like you were all in; it was everything to you. And we're going to talk about what your recent exploration is in that direction of asking questions. Tell us what that looked like for you being all in. Kimber: That's a great question. I'm trying to think of some good examples, but I would say a big example is I served a mission for the church. If you don't know what that is, it's just going out. You get assigned a place and a language. You don't get to choose, and you just spend for girls, it's 18 months. For men, it's two years of your life. Just the sole focus is teaching about Mormonism and trying to convert people to Mormonism. I was a pretty effective missionary. I feel like I've always loved people, and I love talking to people. I was called to serve in New York City, speaking Mandarin Chinese. So, I am fluent in Mandarin, and I ended up minoring in it in college. And it's a really big passion of mine. I was in it my whole life, but that was a part where it just consumed my whole identity, and I think back of other examples of me being devoted, and I think about meeting people who weren't members and not knowing how to interact with them, unless it was in a teaching setting. It was so easy for me to be nice to someone and talk to them, and because I had something to share, but when it came to just regular conversation or not having this pressure. I would just always have this pressure of I need to share the gospel with them. I need to help them understand what they're missing. I remember one of my best friends who she assisted me a little bit on my journey, my faith journey. But she has never been Mormon. Didn't know anything about Mormons, and when I met her, I remember being like, “Oh no, I'm goint to have to invite her to church.” It was just this feeling of like, and I did. I invited her to church within a few weeks of knowing her, and I think it was a really big part of my life. I helped a lot of people get baptized and join the church, and yeah, it's interesting having conversations with those people now. Alexandra: It makes sense if you were raised that way, and as you say, both sides of your family going way way back, that totally makes sense. Kimber: Yeah, and all of our important family conversations at home, extended family, was always centered around church. That was like how we connected and how we could think deeply about things. And if we weren't talking about church or gospel related stuff, it didn't feel as important, and so that was really a big conversation topic in our home. I think part of the reason why I still continue to be really interested in religion. Alexandra: I get it. The cult that I was in, I had that same feeling. I hadn't thought about that in years, but when we were together, we could talk about the deep topics, and that felt so important. Kimber: It's a cool feeling like you're all on the same team, and you all have values and goals. And in Utah, I mean, it's super integrated into the culture, and so it wasn't just my family; it was very reinforced by my neighbors and the people in church every week. I was praised for doing things that, looking back, I'm like we're a little bit intense. I would go up and bear my testimony about not wearing a bikini and how that was so important to not wear a bikini, and I'd speak that to the whole congregation. And then afterwards they're like, “Wow, you're so amazing.” I would talk about how I would tell people, you know, in Sunday school that I didn't date boys who watched rated R movies, and everyone would praise me for that, and so it was a way of like I felt always in the right. And I think that's kind of a damaging mentality to grow up with, as I've learned, to feel always that you know the answers to everything, and you get to teach everyone else. And I think even within Mormonism, I tried to be the very, very, very best example of that. Alexandra: When did your questioning begin, or your exploration? Kimber: I was thinking about this. There's there's a few points that stand out to me. One, I continued to study Mandarin Chinese in college, and I had an opportunity to go to a study abroad in China. I was pretty pretty much the only religious person, let alone Mormon person. I was with a cohort of students that were around my same age, like early 20s, and we all went out and lived in China for two months during a summer, and it was then that I kind of started realizing. I was just so far removed everything. I couldn't go to church. There was no church. You weren't allowed to talk about the gospel out there. I got this paper they sent me. The church sent me that's like you cannot proselyte because that will get you in trouble with the Chinese government, and so just all these things were stripped away. I couldn't proselyte, and I couldn't really talk about my religion, and I also couldn't attend or or practice in the way I was used to. And on top of that, I was surrounded by all these people who were never Mormon and didn't really know what it was. And I feel like that was a time I started to doubt some stuff, and I started to really think about things. I would just try to shut it away, try to shut it away. But I think that was the first time that I really started seriously thinking about things a little bit more. The other thing that comes to mind is getting married. I got married when I was 25, which is pretty old for a Mormon. Everyone's usually getting married at like 20 or 21. In Mormon theology, in order to get to heaven, like the highest level of heaven, you have to be married, and so that was so consuming in my mind. Once I got married, it kind of felt like I'd done everything I needed to do, and I was 25, and so I'd checked off all the boxes. I'm like, great. I get to go to heaven now. Suddenly I had all this mental space to think about other things, and I think my my partner feels the same way. Once we got married, and we moved away immediately from Utah, we moved to Texas actually, and then it kind of gave me some space, similar to China. It gave me space to start thinking about things, and that's when the questioning began. Alexandra: Is your partner Mormon too? Kimber: Yeah, he is. Alexandra: One of the things in your explanation that you talk about, we're going to refer to your Substack quite a bit because that's how I learned a lot about you. On the about page, you talk about navigating a high demand religion, which you would describe Mormonism as, and then but without giving up God. So tell us a little bit. That's a big question. Tell us a little bit about why these two things are important to you. Asking these questions, but also not giving up God. Kimber: When I first started questioning the truth claims of the Mormon Church…I guess for listeners who don't know, Mormonism is very much founded on these certain truth claims that the LDA, the Latter Day Saint Church, is the only true church on the face of the earth. That's one. Two is Joseph Smith was is the founder of the church in 1830 was called by God to be a prophet, and there's a lot that goes into that. And then also the Book of Mormon is the word of God, and the Bible is the word of God as far as it is translated correctly. So, which is like you can only know if it's translated correctly by if the church tells you it's translated correctly. I started questioning these truth claims and looking into the history. I'm a huge researcher, and so I started researching a ton, and I still haven't stopped. There's so much to learn. I think I've been on Substack about three years, which is when I started writing about this. What was really scary to me about even being able to question the church was I was really afraid of losing the parts of myself that I really loved, and that was the spiritual side of things. I loved having conversations about the meaning of life, and I loved thinking about how God could work in my life, and that my life had purpose, and that there was that I wasn't solely in charge of. I don't know how to describe it, but I wasn't just left alone in this world. I had a benevolent being that cared for me, andand so it was really hard for me to start even questioning because I was scared of losing that special relationship I had with God. I think a lot of people in my situation feel that way. They're like, well, I see all these people who question Mormonism, and then they have no religion at all, and don't do anything, and that's not a bad thing. But it was just something that I'm like I was scared of losing it all, I guess. When I started writing, I really tried to focus on on God and tried to focus on this relationship with God and feeling like I belong to God and and I'm going to figure this out with God and then all this other stuff, I'm going to sort through it I guess it's important to me because I used to think that the church, the Mormon Church, and God were synonymous, Alexandra: Right? Kimber: And now I've separated the two, and it's a very clear distinction to me now. But I think for people who read my Substack who are Mormon or in a high demand religion, I want to be approachable for them in a way that's like, look, if you have these beliefs you care about, you get to keep them. Your relationship with God doesn't need to be contingent on a belief in an institution. So, anyway, that's my answer to that. Alexandra: That's awesome, and that's so clear. It is possible to pull those two things apart, and my experience is it can be painful and confusing, and really puzzling and it will really challenge a lot of our beliefs, of course. But it is possible. I can see that in your writing that that's what you're doing. Kimber: I think I was scared of the word deconstruction for a long time because I didn't want everything to just fall, and so I used the word disentangling for that reason. I'm disentangling Jesus out of this, or I'm disentangling God out of this. There's goodness here that I want to keep. And it is really hard, like you said, to separate what you've been taught about who God is and what God cares about, and what you you feel to be more true as you like expand your worldview. Alexandra: Yes, what's important to you? What feels good to you, to the individual, to hang on to. How has writing helped you to do this? Kimber: I would say it's helped me quite a bit. I think a lot of my processing happened through writing, and then I would clean it up a little bit and make it more palatable and less angry, I guess, and more empathetic, and I would post it. I think what really helped me was connecting with other people who are going through the same thing, and even having people in my life who weren't going through the same thing, being able to read it and realize it's something I'm taking seriously. I think in Mormonism there's a lot of phobias around people leaving, and there's things that leadership says about well, they are choosing the easy way, or they just want to drink coffee, or they want to wear cute clothes, and it's like, oh, they're so worldly. I think that for me, writing began as a way of like, hey, if you want to know what I'm actually thinking, you can go and read this. I posted it on my personal Instagram and Facebook, and and my family started reading it, and I think it opened up a lot of conversations with family members, and I think it provided the space for people to be to realize like, I don't know, they they could see that I want people to see this is not an easy thing. It is a really hard thing to leave this mindset and framework, and also like leave a religion that I really loved and devoted my life to. It helps me internally process what was happening, and I also think it helped me find support in my life because if people want to know, they could just go read. Alexandra: Right. When they have done that, what's the response been like? Kimber: The response overall, I would say, is positive. I think I actually wrote about this a little bit a few weeks ago. I wrote a piece called Disentangling Jesus, and it was an essay. And I was just talking about how I'm having to leave behind my certainty to follow God and some of my family members saw as me leaving the church at that time. I was still attending and everything. I almost accidentally said I was leaving, and so people thought that by me saying I'm leaving my certainty, they thought I was leaving my worship. I think that became kind of a scary thing for people in my life. I think specifically, one family member, I actually did write about this later too, but one family member like sent me like super long texts about how I'm deceived by the devil and stuff like that. It's classic, but you know it was validating to get it. I'm like, oh yay. It feels like a big deal. So when everyone is like cool, you're like oh man, it's a big deal. So then when my family member kind of like fought for me, I was like okay, I feel now. But she was like, God lost one of His most valiant soldiers, and all this stuff, and I get it. It brings so much pain for people. I would say at the beginning, I think it was a little bit more polarizing, but now people are more used to it. I also took some of my family members off my mailing list because I think it was causing them distress. So I'm like, this isn't for you. You don't need to read that every week. Alexandra: I'm curious when you go back to Utah to see your family, which I'm assuming you do. Do you go to church? Do you have those conversations at the dinner table? Kimber: So we just actually moved back to Utah like a few months ago. I'm in Utah currently. We were living in Asia for about a year, and then just moved back. And there have been some conversations. I don't go to church normally, but I've been exploring different kinds of churches because I think there is something in me that misses the routine and stability that came with being part of a faith community, and so I've been going to a lot of different churches. I've been to Baptist and non-denominational and Unitarian Universalist, and I can't remember all of them. Orthodox and Catholic and Episcopal and yeah, so many. I've learned so much and it's really fun and Methodist and whatever. I've learned so much from it and it's been really fun. But as far as being here, we haven't really been going to to the LDS Church. Sometimes, if my family is wanting to go, or there's a special event, then we'll go with them. I think overall, it's helped us have better conversations around things like that, where they don't really try to persuade anymore, and I also don't get so reactive about things. Alexandra: That's such an interesting position to be in because you've really announced, via your Substack, where you stand, and what you're exploring and what you're questioning. So your family is aware. I just find that really fascinating. Kimber: It's interesting because when I think back to my childhood, it's like yes, we were super devout, and my parents did this thing that I think really was good. I don't really know why, but for this certain year, we all started going to different churches every week. We would go in addition to the Mormon Church. Mormon Church was three hours, and then we would go to another church, and it was like another hour or two. So it was like five hours of church. But all my siblings and I, we all loved it. We loved seeing how different people were. I think my parents do have a sort of openness because they are curious. They've modeled this curiosity towards other faith traditions. Even though my parents are very devout and strong in their own beliefs and and practices, I do think there's a certain level of of acceptance and openness and that, and it hasn't been like that from the beginning, but has turned into that. Alexandra: That's really cool of them, and that you didn't lose them because of this. Kimber: I know. I think people have different experiences, and right now in Mormonism, there's a lot of people leaving, and so it's becoming way more common for families to learn how to navigate it in healthy ways, and I think that's really positive. But I had an aunt and uncle who left when I was a teenager, and their experience was totally different in my larger family. I think they've been great at being able to support me, and sharing like, yeah, that's it's really hard. Like we get it. It's just been kind of a funny dynamic of being with them and being like, wait, like what side am I on? It's almost like there's a divide in my family. Like am I on the believing or not believing? And I feel like I'm somewhere in the middle, but it's just interesting to. I don't know. It just totally changed how I view my family as well. It's interesting. Alexandra: What you said about exploring other religions, I love that too. When I left the high demand group that I was in, it was actually a therapist who recommended I do that because I was experiencing a lot of loss and grief around not having a faith community or a spiritual community, and so yeah, did a similar thing. I went to Anglican Church and Unitarian Church and United Church, and tried all different kinds of stuff. It was a really good experience, like yours. I really, really enjoyed it, and what lovely people I met, and and then I think, just to talk about myself for two seconds, the caveat I had in the end, I realized that any time spirituality becomes institutionalized, like any time there becomes this group think, I guess you might call it, about what God is or what spirituality is, it put me off. In the end, I just couldn't be a part of any sort of religion. But it was really fun exploring for sure. Kimber: I think for me, it's helped me be okay with the weirdness of Mormonism. I always kind of felt the shame, like, oh wow, being a Mormon is so weird. There's always weird things, like rituals and doctrines and whatever. And then I go to like another, like a Catholic mass, and I'm like, why? Wow, there's kind of some weird stuff there too, and I don't even know all the ins and outs. Eeven like some of these more chill. I guess I don't know if you want to say chill, but like like Unitarian Universalists that are more like accepting, and I go there. They have some weird stuff too. So for me, it's been very validating and helps me feel okay, like we're all kind of weird. I think it's because, like you said, we're trying to capture this feeling and this essence, and trying to make it into an organization, and that's really gets messy. And yeah, when humans are involved, it just gets more complicated because humans are complicated. Alexandra: Absolutely. And you're so right. If you didn't know anything about Catholicism and you observed a mass, I mean, you'd just think it was the wackiest thing. And yet, as you were saying that, it feels like simply because it's been around for so long, it's just become normal,. Mormonism hasn't been around that long, so perhaps that's why it feels a little kookier. Kimber: I think about that a lot. Where I'm like, okay, Mormonism is only, however, like what, 200 years old, maybe a little less. And then I think about that like I don't know, just in thousands of years from now, how are we going to? But also, Mormon is like we're so close to the founding story because it only happened in 1830, right? So it's like we have documents. We have people's affidavits and testimonies and whatever court, whatever. There's so much to Mormon history, but I'm able to read all these primary sources, and that's just something that we don't have when it comes to Christianity or Judaism. We have these traditions that have been passed down from years and years and years, but we're not engaging with the source material. I think about that with Mormonism as like, this is how all religion started, and now it's just become more normalized, or is this like a special case? I don't know. Alexandra: It's such a good question. I think I think we've hit on something there. I wanted to ask: your Substack is called Something on Sundays, correct? Kimber: Something for Sundays. Alexandra: Something for Sundays. Thank you. Is there something about that format that really works for you in terms of the writing that you're doing? What I mean by that is you could have chosen to write a book or to host a podcast, or so. What is it about Substack that works for you? Kimber: I think overall, what I really have liked about being on Substack is I've always written a blog since I was like 12. I just have always been writing something. My Substack used to be called Kimber Was Here, and I was compiling all of my writings, like poems and past blog posts. I've kind of just been in different spaces on the internet, and I'm like, okay, I'm just going to put them all together on this substack. Then I started writing more regularly about some of the traveling and everything that we're doing, and then when all this questioning started happening, it just became a natural outlet for me. I majored in English, so I've just really liked writing. I chose the name Something for Sundays because Sundays was a very special day to me all growing up. It was always filled. I always knew what I was going to be doing on Sunday, and I had a very specific routine of going to church and coming home and taking a three-hour nap and then eating family dinner. Then when I started to distance myself from the church, I found like you were describing a loss and a grief around Sundays. Like what am I going to do this Sunday, or what am I going to go to a different church, am I just going to lay in bed? Am I going to listen to a sermon or online? There's so many different things you do. So I started to write Something for Sundays as kind of a thing of being like, okay, this is something for my Sunday, and it's something for your Sunday if you're in the same position as me. It's kind of turned into something special. Every week I give little recommendations; something to read, something to watch, something to try, something to make. I'll choose a few each week, and so that gives people something to do on Sunday. With Substack. I also have been really enjoying doing more illustration, and so I create illustrated essays. I do them like I try to do it once a month. They take a little bit more time, so it just depends. I started illustrating some of my experiences, and I started exploring different ways of communicating what I was going through, and also just what I've been thinking about. I think Substack has a platform that can hold all of that, which I like. Alexandra: I was reading your post from yesterday. We're recording this on a Monday, and it was about a sidewalk chalk event that you had done with your sister, which was really cool. The post is called “Done, not perfect.” You talk about how completing things and how doing them is more important than making them perfect. And I really encourage people to read it because it was really deep and thoughtful about what it means to be perfect versus good. You talk about that and refer to East of Eden, which you say is one of your favorite books. The thing that really resonated with me was how easy it can be to not try to do something because we think it has to be perfect. I just wanted to bring that up and point it out because I think when people are new to writing, they can stop themselves because they think it's not going to be good enough, it's not going to be perfect, and that kind of thing. One of the things I like about blogs and places like Substack is that it feels like there's less expectation to be perfect. Would you agree? Kimber: Yeah, for sure. I think because of the frequency of it, if you choose to write weekly or monthly, like there's definitely times where I've been like, this is done, not perfect. Just send it out there. I think kind of what you're saying, like feeling not good enough to start or not good enough to to put it out there. One of my favorite books is East of Eden, like you mentioned. Another favorite book is The Artist's Way by Julia Cameron. Have you done that? It's just amazing. I did it last year, and she talks about audacity is what brings an artist to the center stage faster, or even more so than talent. It's all about audacity, and that has just really resonated with me in all areas of my life. When I was reading that book, I applied to Harvard Divinity School, and I did all these things. I had all this audacity of I'm just going to try it. I'm going to paint. I'm going to do this and that. I'm going to write, and I think there's all these things I did and I tried that I would not have tried if I was so caught up in it has to be perfect. Something I've been thinking about a lot recently is I think I just try to intellectualize everything. I'm intellectualizing like okay I want to paint an oil I want to get into oil painting for example and then so I'm going to watch a bunch of tutorials and I'm going to sign up for a really expensive class. I'm going to research all the materials to buy, and then I'm going to buy them, and then I'm going to buy better ones. It's like I keep procrastinating the actual doing of it, and I feel like that's totally how it can be with writing too. I started buying writing courses and started buying like books and all this stuff, and then I kind of stopped writing as frequently because I started feeling like, wait, I'm not doing all these things that they're suggesting, and I'm not having a perfect writing routine. I think there's value in those kind of books, like teaching you how to write or teach you how to be creative, but I think when you use that as a form of procrastination from starting the actual thing is when, at least for me, I start to get really anxious. It's like all this pent up potential with no outlet, and so that's what I have to think about. I think with writing, like you're saying, it is a really cool way to process. Same with drawing, like process and just make visual and make real what's happening internally. I definitely feel it's important to just just do it, just go for it. Alexandra: Exactly, and we can't get better until we do. So if we prevent ourselves from doing the thing, then we won't ever improve. Kimber: I fall into that a lot. I don't know your whole experience with the cult you were a part of, but at least in Mormonism, there's a very high focus on perfection, and it's like they are constantly telling you like you will never be perfect, but you have to try. I get that. But then, if you're hearing that, and that's the core message every single week for 20 years, it just gets in you, and it manifests itself in the culture a lot. Plastic surgery is like the highest per capita in Utah. Alexandra: Oh wow! Kimber: Yeah, so it's like that's just an example. GLP one, plastic surgery, all these cosmetic things. I think it's a reflection of this belief system because everyone is yeah. Anyway, we can go into Utah culture, but I do think it's an internal thing for sure, like perfectionism. Alexandra: My experience with the cult I was in was there was an expectation of perfection, but the goalposts were always moved, so you could never actually get there, and any fault that occurred was always with the person, the individual. Kimber: Totally. Have you ever read “Combating Cult Mind Control” by Steve Hassan. He talked about that, about how that's like a common thing that cults will do is like make it be your fault, and I've been thinking about that a lot. What's the use of that? The use of that is they create a problem, and then they also create the solution, right? And that's like a common marketing tactic. I think about I see all these billboards everywhere of plastic surgery and it's like you know it's like they create a problem like oh my nose isn't like this turned up thing you know and then it's it makes me feel like oh maybe I need to get a nose job because I have the solution as well. I think I think a lot of high demand religions work in that in that same framework Alexandra: Yes. I think that's a classic manoeuvre for sure. I had this question that I had sent you in advance about what you've learned about yourself and your beliefs. We've talked about that a little bit with this exploration that you've been on. Is there anything else you can think of that really come to light for you? Kimber: I think the biggest thing I've learned about myself, my beliefs. The biggest thing I've learned about myself is that I can show up for something again and again, week after week, for a few years, and I can be really consistent. I think that's something that I've learned about myself. I didn't know I was really capable of that. I'm really proud of of being able to show up for myself and show up for the people who read Something for Sundays, and I think as far as beliefs go, I think I've come to really value uncertainty in the sense of, I really value the mystery of life, which was definitely not the case before. I think when I was really in Mormonism, like really fully in it, I felt better than everyone because I knew everything about the inner workings of the world and the universe. Now I've really become more comfortable with this mystery and being curious. I think I really value people who are curious as well, and kind of what you were talking about when you were saying that you went to the different faith traditions and ultimately decide that wasn't for you. I think that I get that because whenever I've gone somewhere and they say something like so definitive, it instantly is like a red flag for me. Where I'm like, wait a second. How do they know that? What are they basing it on? I've really learned how to think critically, and I think writing has helped me with that. That process of if I'm going to write something, and you can kind of see it if you read my really early things. I'm a little bit more preachy, which is just how I was back then, and I've definitely through the years have become a lot more like less willing to just be like, well, this is what I believe, and this is why it's right. It''s been yeah, it's been interesting. Alexandra: That's so cool. We are just about out of time, so as we start to wrap up, is there anything we haven't touched on that you'd like to share with our listeners? Kimber: I think one other thing is recently I started doing a zine, so it's like a mini magazine, and it has illustrations and writing in it, and that's been a fun new way, a new creative pursuit that I've done. That's kind of brought Something for Sundays into a physical subscription form. I did that one because I didn't want to turn on paid subscriptions on Substack, but I was getting to the point where it was taking a lot of time, and so I was trying to think of a new way to maybe supplement some of my time with money and and so I started this this zine. It's been really fun and exciting. I send it out to people all over all over the country and actually internationally as well. So that's something I think is my creative pursuit recently. That is fun. I think along those lines, I would want people to know that you don't need to box yourself into one thing. If you are creative in one way, you can be creative in another way too. Like if you really like singing and playing music, that doesn't mean you're not going to enjoy painting. You don't have to be good at it. You can just try it, and you might be surprised that that can actually assist in your music. That's just an example of I think as you use your creativity, it benefits other areas of your life as well. Alexandra: Well said. Yeah, that's amazing. All right. Please tell us where we can find out more about you and your writing. Kimber: My Substack is Somethingforsundays.substack.com, and I'm also on Instagram, Something for Sundays, and my mail club is something for Sundays club. So it's all something for Sundays related. If anyone is interested in the zine, something for Sundays club is where you can learn more about that. Those are my main three places that I update. Alexandra: Awesome. I'll put links in the show notes to those three things. Kimber: Thank you so much. Alexandra: Well, thank you, Kimber. This has been a delight. It's been so nice talking to you. Kimber: Nice talking to you too. Thank you for having me. Click here to grab your complimentary copy of the Creative Alchemy journaling handbook. episodes.title: Finding Healing in Gender Transition with Comedy with Patti Savard
episodes.description: Vancouver Island comedian Patti Savard also happens to be a transgender woman. She brings the subject of gender transition into her comedy. So the biggest question I had for her was, how do we laugh at something that is often perceived as being a very serious subject? I think you'll appreciate her answer. In the introduction, I mention the unique early morning writing practice that Patti talks about during the interview. And I touch on how this conversation made clear to me how important it is for all of us to allow our creative expression to be what it wants to be. We don't need to fit ourselves into a predetermined type of creativity. By its very nature, creativity is freedom and expresses itself in infinite ways. We do ourselves a favour when we allow that expression to take any form it wishes. Patti Savard is a Canadian comedian and comedy cabaret performer based in the Comox Valley, British Columbia. Blending stand-up, storytelling, theatrics, and song, Patti creates bold, heartfelt performances that explore identity, belonging, and the strange hilarity of being human. Her one-woman comedy cabaret, Life in Transition, combines razor-sharp wit with disarming honesty as Patti shares stories of living authentically in spaces one wouldn't expect acceptance of a transwoman. Patti has performed at the Vancouver Just For Laughs Festival and was selected to present Life in Transition at the Glasgow International Comedy Festival, where the show has been nominated for the Sir Billy Connolly Spirit of Glasgow Award. Her work resonates with audiences through humour, vulnerability, and a joyful celebration of authenticity. You can learn more about Patti at her Instagram: pattisavard18 This episode of Creative Alchemy is supported by the audiobook version of my award-winning, Amazon best-selling memoir, Cult, A Love Story. Readers call the book 'compelling' 'gritty' 'intimate' and 'not boring' – which is what an author loves to hear. I narrated the audiobook and if you have a Spotify premium subscription you can listen to the audiobook for free as part of that subscription at alexandraamor.com/spotify . You can listen above, on your favorite podcast app , or watch on YouTube . Notes, links, resources and a full transcript are below. Show Notes Performing stand-up for the very first time with three days notice Using comedy as a way to seek acceptance Developing a joke writing practice Receiving mentoring around comedy craft Getting honest feedback from a live audience How comedy is about connection with the audience On writing jokes about the potentially serious subject of gender transition Changing minds and hearts through comedy How working through comedic material to make it authentic brings healing Using dreams as a springboard for creative expression How 'weird' is a beautiful expression of humanity Finding healing in helping others Resources mentioned in this episode Iconic Canadian tv show, Corner Gas Syd Bosel , comedian Eddie Murphy's stand-up comedy film, Delirious Transcript of the interview with Patti Savard Alexandra: Patti Savard, welcome to Creative Alchemy. Patti: Thank you for having me. Alexandra: It's so good to see you. Tell a little bit about who you are and a bit about your background. Patti: All righty. I am a comedian from the Comox Valley up in Courtenay. I've been doing it for going on five years now. I've performed in Toronto's Massey Hall. I've performed in Just for Laughs, Vancouver. This year, I performed in Glasgow, Scotland, at the Glasgow International Comedy Festival, and I was nominated for the Sir Billy Connolly Award, which was kind of cool. I absolutely love that man's comedy. What a fantastic storyteller! So, to have a nomination associated to that guy's name really feels good. Other than that, I am a carpenter. I run my own business because I'm a Canadian comedian, and five years at this game. I don't know how to tip the scales, but I don't want to be a starving artist. And since I have skills, I am happy to use them. I'm a parent also, and I also have to make sure that I'm taking care of their financial obligations that fall on me. Alexandra: I hear you about the starving artist part. I don't have the answer to how you can tip the scales either. I don't know about that. Patti: It'll come all things in time. I don't know, or I don't know. I keep doing goofy stuff at work too, so at least I'm not getting lost in the process. I bought a a Kool Aid Man costume, and if you go on my Instagram, you'll see a video of me running through a wall wearing that suit as I'm doing demolition, which I have written off on my taxes as a business expense because it's for comedy purposes and for business purposes, it's my demolition suit now. Alexandra: Exactly. Oh, that's great. I wonder if you could write that off twice. Wouldn't that be good? Patti: I think that's illegal, but um, but okay. Alexandra: I saw you first when you gave a comedy show coordinated through a group that I belong to called Island Queers and Allies Who Care, and that was my first exposure to your work. And one of the things that really struck me was that you talk about your transition in comedy, and so I'm just wondering how that started. Let's start at the beginning. Tell us about when you felt comfortable to start doing that. Patti: Sounds good. I actually started performing stand-up comedy right after transition, relatively immediately. It was a way of trying to see in front of a large group of people how I would be received as a human, but also, I think the entire process is very funny. I was born in 1983, and so the the concept of transitioning from one gender to another is ludicrous in terms of all the beliefs that I was taught and everything, and so I think the whole act of it is brilliantly funny. I thought using comedy as a way of trying to force people to receive me was very effective, and it worked out. Yeah, so it it all started right at that moment. Actually, as COVID came to an end, it was the very first event to happen in the Comox Valley. Right at that moment when we were allowed to have, I think up to 100 people in a space or something like that. Somebody organized an open mic comedy night, and I went and did it. And it was packed. There were literally exactly 100 people there, and I got really great laughs, and I became addicted. Alexandra: Had you always been a fan of comedy up to that point? Patti: Definitely, but not so much of a follower. I'd actually never been to a comedy show before. Alexandra: You're kidding! Oh my god! Wow! Where did you begin? How did you start writing jokes and that kind of stuff? Patti: Well, that week, I guess. In comedy, there's the rule of threes, which is you know there's certain jokes that you tell them like series of three things together, and usually works out if it's a good joke. I was working at a brewery in Comox. That's another story on its own. I was having a bad day, and I just kind of joked around to myself because I was working by myself to try to make my day lifted, and I was like, “That's kind of funny. Maybe I should write it down, because maybe if I'm having a bad day, I could just look at these stupid things I've written, and just cheer myself up.” About an hour later, an older gentleman was walking past the brew house on the sidewalk and to my open garage door that I had there, and I started just goofing around with the guy, and he was like, “You're so funny. You should be on Corner Gas.” Which, as a Canadian, is a very strange reference. It's very directly Canadian. But again, it was like, “Oh, you think I'm funny too?” And then my ex wife, well, we were married at the time. She came into the brew house another hour beyond that, and she said, “Hey, did you hear that? There's an open mic comedy night happening at the other brewery in Courtney.” She told me that because being like, “Hey, that means we can have events now too,” but I took it as I should go perform at that. So I wrote down everything that I thought was funny, and then three days later, I was up on the stage. Alexandra: Really, holy cow! And you said you got lots of laughs, so it was received well. Patti: It was, yeah. I mean, considering I only had a few days to write the jokes, they went okay. But like I said, the whole transition process is funny. So those jokes were up in the old vault. I just had to pull them out. Alexandra: It was stuff that you had been thinking of that was absurd for a while. It sounds like. Patti: Yeah, because I think life is a joke. Everything is a joke, and and and if you just have to see it. Alexandra: I want to talk about courage then. Being creative can require a lot of courage, and it's something that people can avoid at times because it feels like maybe it requires too much of them, too much courage, too much exposure, that kind of thing. Did you feel like it required courage from you to do this, or did you just take the leap? Patti: No, because you know, like telling my mom that I was trans and my dad, and like, oh yeah, my stepdad, just like my all my family, that was so hard, and so after once that was done, I was just like, I can do anything. Got it. Alexandra: Everything pales in comparison to that. It sounds like. Patti: Mind you. If you threw me in the middle of the ocean, without a boat, I'd probably be losing it. Alexandra: Do you have a practice? So that first show was really put together quickly. Did you develop a practice after that of writing jokes? Patti: Yes, I did. Fortunately, some of the other comedians were new to the Comox Valley and looking to start a comedy scene here. And since I had that brewery space, not the one that we did the open mic at, but the one that I was working in. I said, “You know, we could run a regular occurring open mic to try to get more people out and and start a bit of a scene here.” We started doing that – a monthly open mic, and then eventually a monthly showcase. And so for me, it gave me a reason to write because you know, once a month, I got to get up on the mic, and it's the same people, so I can't just say the same jokes every time, which is also a trap. I don't want to say that that's a good idea for new comedians. I think the best thing to do is write your best five minutes, and that means perform that same five minutes over and over and over again, so that you can crack the code on making it really funny. But it also is a good idea to write some different stuff here and there. And so I kind of did that. I wrote a few different five-minute sets. About a year later, there was a comedy competition in Vancouver, and I decided to enter it. And then one of my good friends, Syd Bosel, who is a local comedian here, she's kicking it. But in the comedy scene right now, she's on CBC Debaters. She's super good. She was just like, hey, why don't you send me what you think is your best seven minutes, and I will go over it. Then we'll go over it together, and we'll work it down to what your best five is, because she wants to get more into comedy mentoring. I could totally use the mentorship, and so she showed me a few techniques that I've taken with me to this day in terms of writing, and yeah, I'm grateful for that. Absolutely. Alexandra: Sometimes I hear about comedians talk about working out stuff on stage. I heard Tig Notaro say that just recently. She figures out what she's doing and what's funny while she's on stage. It sounds to me like you maybe do a bit more preparation beforehand. Is that true? Patti: Yes, that is true. I am definitely a relatively scripted performer. A lot of us are, and the key or craft behind being a scripted person is to make it look like it's not scripted. That being said, if you learn your stuff really well, that also allows you to sit in the zone, which is basically what Tig is referring to, where you just are in that full zone of comfort, and you just allow to come to you what comes. If I get up there without a book on the stage, so I don't look at my. We often throw a book out there, especially if it's an open mic or something like that, where you're working out new stuff, just to make sure you hit your beats. You don't read your full word for word. You just name the joke. You write the joke, then you name it, so you can see the name. So, if you ever find a book on the streets and it's just random statements that make no sense from one to the other, and they're a little bit inappropriate, it's probably a comedian stage book. I tend to be a little bit more on the scripted side, but the more that I've gotten to know my material, the less scripted I'm becoming. If that makes any sense, because I already know the jokes and I know what I want to say next. But sometimes in the moment, because of an interaction with somebody in the audience, for instance, it makes me say something different, and then that makes me want to change the direction, and then I say something else instead, and I will fall back into the jokes. I'm sure Tig does it too. I mean, there's no way that she's entirely unscripted. What she's referring to is when you go up on stage and you already have written the things in your head, and you just go you pull it from your head. But that's a long way of saying that. Alexandra: Was this something you could ever imagine yourself doing when you were younger? Patti: Yes, actually, I remember when I was a little kid. Firstly, when I was a kid, I knew that I always wanted to be a girl, like from the age of four, basically. But I believed that to be impossible, and that it was actually that belief system or that thought that I had was potentially a mental illness, and so if I did not allow myself to indulge in it, then I would not become mentally ill. I remember watching Eddie Murphy's Delirious and just finding it so funny, and just just being jealous of him doing that. I almost pictured myself almost the opposite of being like an Arnold Schwarzenegger muscular kind of person up on stage and making jokes about it being like you wouldn't expect somebody that to be funny because they just look so big and brash and all that kind of stuff, which is I suppose a touch ironic. If that's actually ironic, no, I don't really know what ironic actually is. It doesn't matter. Schwarzenegger is funny, actually, brilliantly funny. But so, but anyhow, that that that was, yeah, I did think about it, but I was like, never. I'll never do that. Never in a million years. Alexandra: It sounds like you admired the artists that were doing it at the time. Patti: Oh gosh, yes. Eddie Murphy was one of my favorites, and then Robin Williams, later like Sarah Silverman, and Mitch Hedberg eventually became my favorite of the favorites. Now these days, John Mulaney. But truthfully, I don't really watch much stand-up. If I'm not performing on stage with you, I probably haven't seen your material. I just don't watch things in general. Alexandra: How did you learn? So you did that very first open mic night three days out, after you had the idea, and then what? Did you watch instructional videos on YouTube or read books? Patti: Well, practice, write a joke, practice the joke, go up on stage and do the joke. Take the honest feedback from the audience. Go home, work, rework what didn't work. Take it back to the stage. Take the honest feedback, and do that until the joke murders. Alexandra: Wow. Okay, I'm just reflecting on being a novelist and someone who writes books, I never really have to expose myself to that kind of immediate feedback from people. That takes courage, I think. Patti: We thrive on it. That is what the art form is. Every once in a while, you get a gift from the universe. You get a joke where you write this, you perform it, and it just crushes, and you never have to change the words. That's like a a gem. I actually have a joke that I wrote three years ago that always did pretty well, but I I knew it needed something different, and actually, just last week, I reworked the joke entirely, and all of a sudden, now it's doing what I want it to do, and that's three years. Alexandra: Wow! I didn't realize one could do that. That's really extraordinary. Patti: Well, it's really about the audience connection, and so that's I think why we write this way is because comedy is very subjective. What is funny to you might not be funny to everybody else, and so if a joke falls apart, it's usually lacking in about in three things: clarity, contrast, or shit. What's the other? It's 3c's. It makes it easier to remember, but it's not working for me right now. Clarity, contrast, and compression. If you're too wordy, sometimes you know somebody goes on a bit, right? So usually one of those things is what makes a joke land. If it's tight in all those three areas and context, there's a fourth C, but I don't know whatever C's. Just we'll just throw C words at it. Alexandra: We've talked about feedback, and one of the things I wanted to ask you was what the reception has been like from people about you joking about what can be quite a serious subject: transitioning from one gender to the other. What's that been like? Patti: Well, therein lies the beauty of comedy, and that and one of the C's contrast. What beautiful contrast it is, right? It is a very touching, emotionally very personal subject, and so it gets the audience's attention because not a lot of people are very familiar with it. These days, it seems like most families have somebody in that or who's trans; that could be a cousin or whatever. Maybe not in your household, but it's becoming more common now. Not because we are changing in that respect, but because we're feeling more safe to come out, and so our very degrees of transness are now rising to the surface. That being said, it gets the audience's attention. It does cut. The hard part for me is when it's not working. If I have an audience that's tightening up, and if I can't shake them I just stand up there and I basically tell really personal things to people, and they give me nothing back. And that, well, as a comedian, you get used to it because everybody bombs. Alexandra: Yes, yes, of course. I think of the performance that I saw that I mentioned earlier. I would consider that audience to be kind of warm. They were all involved with or aware of the organization that was organizing it, and that it was queer focused. In that performance, you talked about performing in bars in Taber, Alberta. That must require another set of skills. Patti: Yes, and I think my first year into comedy, I probably would have cried after performing in places like that. Because I approached it like well, it was last summer that I was in in rural Alberta, Red Deer, Taber, a bunch of places, but you know rural, on the more conservative side of Canada. My strategy going in, well, I have what a lot of well, there's a term referred to as passing privilege that that we use. Where I mean, those who can't see me, I don't know if this is a visual podcast or just audio, but if they can't see me, my voice might give me away a bit, but not necessarily. And so, I have strengthened my non-trans subject matter material. When I get up on the stage, I just get up and I get them to like me as a comedian first. And the longer I can go without having to touch on the subject, the more trust I get with the audience, and then I cut their legs off. And so I then I out myself as trans, and then I have to pick up the pieces again. 99% of the time it works out, and it's because you like me already. So if you don't like me now, there's something up with you. And this is something I'm starting to now strengthen a little bit. Now is when I out myself at this point, if the audience still tightens up on me, as long as the material was working before I outed myself. Then I can start crowd working them, and just being like, “Oh, you look really uncomfortable. How are you feeling right now?” And then lean on the other audience members who are laughing, and try to pull their laughter towards that person, so hopefully they can crack loose. It's interesting. It pulls some interesting energies out of the room, but you know, comedy's all about discomfort and then cracking it. Alexandra: You're making me realize, and I had just had no idea how many skills are required really in what you're doing. There's the courage of getting on stage, which for some people like me would be virtually impossible. And then you're talking about there's so many other skills that you're having to use, and I imagine those have gradually built up over time. Patti: Yeah, with the performance skills, definitely. But a lot of those are life skills too. Just like navigating this world as a human being. I feel like I give credit to whatever it is that you do in life, whenever you take on your next endeavor, because something else that you've already done will give you a skill that you didn't realize was associated to that craft. Thinking about everything that you do in life, pull all those things together, and I think it helps and it goes a long way. Comedy's not easy. Drag queens get so many tips. I think comedians need to get tips too. We have to figure out how to do that. Alexandra: It's not fair. That's very true. Do you feel that comedy is healing? Patti: 100% for me, and absolutely for sometimes audiences that I've gotten to perform to, which is really neat. Alexandra: Has anyone ever approached you after a show and said that you've changed their mind about things. Patti: That exact statement which you just said. Yes, I was in Salmon Arm, British Columbia, and there was a couple in the front row. They were definitely on the redneck side. You know, but I really joked around with them a lot, and I mean, my dad is such a redneck, you know. So I get rednecks. There's definitely a tan on my neck too. At the end of the show, the woman came up to me and she said, “I gotta say, I've had a lot of negative experiences with trans people, and you changed my mind today. The way that you brought up your material was just so approachable to the subject.” I think I'm using better English than she did. She was a very confrontational human. I imagine everybody in the world that you encounter seems to be a mirror of yourself to some degree. So, I imagine if she had negative encounters with trans people, it's probably the way she approached it in the first place, and vice versa with the people that she was encountering. That kind of thing happens often, and it's my favorite part, especially in the rural parts of the country. Usually, I get discussions that are just so raw and real, or somebody asking me questions. I had a grandmother come up to me afterward, and I was so worried about doing this show in the first place because it was a bar, and I'm like, okay, I'm gonna do a few dirty jokes tonight. But there was a table of very old women that were clearly out for a nice night, and I did a few off color jokes about anatomy and things, and I was like, “Oh my God, I can't believe I did that.” At the end of the show, one of them came up to me, and she was just like, “Well, firstly we loved your show.” And I'm like, “Yes, you did. You guys laughed a lot.” And she's just like, “But you know, I have a grandchild who's trans, and I've been afraid to ask a lot of questions. And so just the stuff that you said like really made me feel more comfortable about how to approach things.” I love that a lot. Alexandra: It feels like soft diplomacy almost, doesn't it? Patti: I like that term. Alexandra: That's great. Oh, and good for her. Getting back to the subject of courage; good for her for having an open mind and for acknowledging her grandchild and wanting to know more. Patti: Yes, and this is another fascinating thing too-a beautiful thing, really-is one of the main reasons why I tour the rural aspects of the country. Firstly, I have the privilege, so I can kind of go undercover until I decide to out myself. But, I believe that there's more love out there than the news wants you to know. And so far, I see nothing but this come forward. I definitely have the odd encounter, which isn't awesome, but that's few and far between, and the majority of people are like opening their minds, and their hearts, really. So it is nice. Alexandra: We touched on healing. Do you feel like there are specific things about your experience or your feelings that have been healed by working on this craft of comedy? Patti: Absolutely, yeah. I was reviewing some of my older stand up videos just to study notes and things, and I noticed my hyper feminization when I first started this four years ago. The amount of hyperfeminization of my voice, the mannerisms a bit too. I kind of had to, like over the past few years for myself, accept that some masculine parts within me are actually part of me and don't need to be shoved back under the rug, which is kind of like like a teeter-totter game of basically that's what I was doing. When I lived 30 something years of suppressing everything feminine, and then as soon as I let it rise, that masculine side fell all the way down, and I kind of had to scale it off and accept all parts of myself. I believe we all have a bit of masculine and feminine energy. I've got way more feminine energy than I do masculine energy, but it needed to be allowed too. That was a big part of my healing journey that came through with this. Talking about it on stage about these really personal aspects of myself, and then having to rework the material one so that I could believe in it, because in order to believe in it, I had to feel it, which is what actors do with their craft too. I had to truly feel it and own it, and that process itself brought the healing. Alexandra: That visualization of the teeter totter is so great. What I pictured as you were talking about it was sort of the extreme swings, and that what I think what you're pointing to is that gradually they come into balance. They're not tipping so much one side or the other. Patti: Absolutely. I think that general state of weak equilibrium of what my normal is is kind of what that what that means, absolutely. Alexandra: I can really understand how tricky that would be when you've spent however many decades pushing that feminine part of yourself away. It would take some time and some doing to find that balance. Patti: No doubt. I think you know, for those first couple of years after transition, I really had to let her shine. So I think he had to stay under the rug. I think he did it okay. But then I started having dreams-a lot of dreams-with masculine energy around fire, like just like a lot of visualizations, and with this power, and I wanted to have the fire power that they could have. Dreams are so metaphorical, and my dreams were actually a big part of what showed me that too. Is just that suppression of self was the limitation on finding that kind of power. I part of my writing process is I write down my dreams in the morning. They're fascinating, and it puts me in creative writing mode. After I finish writing them, I'm already in the creative spirit, and then I can start. Hopefully, jokes are what come next. Sometimes they're not, but when they are, it's great. And so yeah, that dream state part. I forgot what the question was, but I think I answered it. Alexandra: Yes, you did. Thank you. On that note of writing practice, do you do that every morning? Write down your dreams. Patti: I do. I wake up much earlier than I need to before work, and I write down my dreams. It takes usually about 20 minutes or so, and then right after that, whatever the finishing thought was after writing out the dreams is usually what I carry forward. Then I go into just free writing, just write whatever comes to mind, or sometimes there'll be a joke that I was working on yesterday, and then I'll be like, “Oh, okay, let's write on that now.” A writer-I forget her name-but she said that when you're in the zone, when you're writing, stop yourself like before you're done. So right when you're still in the gist of it and you want to keep going, but it's been a good amount of time, just deliberately stop, and it kind of keeps that thread active for next time. And so I've started trying to adapt that a little bit. Alexandra: Nice, and that works for you. Patti: It seems to. I mean, I'm consistently getting new material or or writing strengthening notes on other stuff, and it seems to help out a lot. I mean, there are just those moments too where you're out doing something, and I'm like, oh, I've got to write this down. Most comedians are that way. If something just happens, we'll drop what we're doing. Like in the middle of a conversation, I'll be like, I'm really sorry, but I have to write this down. Alexandra: I've seen musicians refer to that as well, and carry little notebooks around with little snippets of ideas. I keep ideas in my phone sometimes too, and that helps. Patti: Me too. I use a phone also. Alexandra: I think I've heard Elizabeth Gilbert talk about that, finishing before the thread is finished, and then picking it up the next day. But I don't think she's the only person who's said that. Patti: I don't remember. I didn't write the person's name down, but maybe it was her. I don't know. Alexandra: As we're coming toward the end of our conversation here: Is there anything that surprised you about this career and the comedy that you offer to the world? Patti: Good question. I think the thing that surprised me is how small the comedy community is here in Canada. I found that to be rather interesting. I mean, it's growing a lot, especially since COVID and and there's a lot of people getting into stand-up now, but that was definitely one aspect. Just how connecting it can be due to that too.. I've got friends across the country, just because we share this instinct to get in our car and drive three hours to perform 15 minutes. Sometimes even less. I don't really know what else. I suppose just how much it's connected to my life itself. Actually, here's one: the types of friends that I'm making. I feel like comedians are misfits. We're all just a group of people put together. I play a lot of sports. Or you're a computer guy who sits at a desk. We would not be friends if it wasn't for this, but our brains all have this weird thing. We look at the world in a bizarre way. That it was a surprising thing is the more you talk to comedians we seem to have brains that function in a just an interesting way. A different way of looking at the world. I mean the fact that we're trying to find the joke in everything means that you can go super dark, or you can go really light, or you can go really goofy, or there's so many different aspects of it. Those things are definitely a bit surprising. That's a question I'm gonna have to sit on a lot more though too. What else has surprised me? But I don't know. That doesn't help with this interview. Alexandra: That's great. Thank you. What has the response been from the trans community to your comedy, if any? Patti: I run a monthly show in Nanaimo called “Bring Out Your Weird”, and it's a comedy cabaret variety show I did at the Vault Cafe on the last Thursday of the month. And the premise of that show is: if you are weird, consider yourself weird, have a weird performance, showcase yourself. Weird is just a beautiful expression of humanity, and I think being trans naturally falls into that. I was asked to join Comox Valley Pride, which I did a few years ago. Being a trans spokesperson, I guess, so to speak, I've done a lot of performing within my community, and so I've been asked to show leadership in ways. I no longer am on the board because it was just too much work, and I am so not political. But I still perform in functions like, for instance, just coming up this weekend is Comox Valley Pride, and so I'm going to be doing performing at a couple things there. I would like to think that I'm helping mentor some of the younger trans kids and folks who are finding themselves. The QSA in the Comox Valley. That's the Queer Straight Alliance. They asked me to speak a couple times at their functions to the kids, as well as they do a Pride prom, which is oh my god, such a beautiful thing. It's once a year. After COVID, there was no prom because the prom committees all just stopped doing it, and so the QSA said, “Hey, why don't we organize it? It'll be for everybody, but it'll be organized by the queer kids.” Naturally, the queer kids thought to throw a party first. Just saying. But every year I do trivia with them. I usually just make up some dumb game, and I do it at their intermission at the halfway point. It is so fabulous getting to be there as an adult, as somebody who's openly trans and out there, watching these kids who are feeling free to express themselves at a school type function. For me it helped. That helps heal my own trauma, that trauma of not being able to express myself back in those ages. It's just so amazing to get to watch them do it, and I literally heal every time I'm there. It's great. I'd say I'm playing my part in my community, doing my best to. But we're healing each other. Alexandra: Oh, that's a lovely way to say it. That's amazing, beautiful. As we come toward the end of this interview, is there anything you wanted you'd like to share that we haven't touched on yet? Patti: Oh, what haven't we touched on? I mentioned that I've got a monthly show in Nanaimo. And I don't know. People just follow comedy and comedians. We need the support. We need lots of it. You can follow my social media stuff. I'm PattiSavard18 at Instagram. That's my social media. I don't post a lot of videos because I'm currently working on my comedy album, and so I'm just kind of holding the material back until I do that. But I do a lot of self-promotion on there. I do post a lot of video content from the Bring Out Your Weird show because on that one I do a lot of ridiculous things. I'm not just a stand up, and the beauty of this show that Bring Out Your Weird is a concept is that I get to do whatever I want. So this week's show, for instance, I will be singing Alanis Morissette's Ironic, but I've rewritten the words to make the song actually ironic, just for fun. I do a lot of dumb, silly antics that are just ridiculous, just because I can. I think for whatever people, everybody is a creative person, and I think I want everybody to realize they're a creative person. So yeah, that's something I really want to say. If I'm just getting to know somebody, if I go to a pride function or something, and I'm having a conversation with, I hate small talk. I hate small talk. So I'll just say, “What do you do creatively? And then sometimes they'll say, “I'm not creative.” I'll say, “Yes, you are. What is it that you've done that's creative in the past?” They often have to rack their brain, but they'll come up with something like, “Oh, I used to write poetry.” I'll ask, “Oh, what made you stop?” actually had that exact conversation with somebody, and then I saw her six months later, and I was just like, “Hey, so what are you doing creatively?” And she's like, “I'm writing poetry.” I'm like, yay! Alexandra: Well done, wow, that's awesome. I totally agree. Everybody is creative, and that's one of the reasons this podcast exists. Patti: Amazing. Alexandra: Thank you for reminding us about that. This has been lovely. I will put links in the show notes to your Instagram, and is there a link I could put in for the Bring Out Your Weird Show? Patti: That is in the top notes of my Instagram. There's always a link there to the current show. And that one's monthly, so I don't know when this will be aired, but so I'm not sure if it'll be aired before that show or not. Alexandra: Okay, I'll make sure there's a link to your Instagram in the show notes. Patti: Wonderful. Alexandra: Thank you, Patti. It's been lovely talking to you. Patti: It's been so lovely talking to you as well. Thank you so much for having me. Alexandra: You're so welcome. All right. Take care. Patti: You too.
