episodes.title: Taking Ownership of Your Story with Hanna Etu
episodes.description: Every human appreciates knowing they are not alone. When we have an experience – perhaps one of being in a cult or being an addict or being a single mother – we all want to know we are not alone in that experience. Two of the most powerful and reassuring words in the English language are “me too”. My guest today, Hanna Etu, works with neurodivergent and mad writers, supporting them to tell their stories so that others may find comfort in knowing they're not alone. In the introduction, I talk about how I connected with Hanna's work shepherding books, particularly memoirs, into the world. And how my memoir, Cult, A Love Story , came into being because of an unmet need I had to read someone's personal story of being in a cult. Hanna Etu helps mad and neurodivergent writers establish a regular writing practice so they can finish their memoirs without losing the heart of their story. She has a book coaching certification in memoir and nonfiction from Author Accelerator. Her degrees in Creative Writing and English as well as a professional background in traditional book publishing give her unique insight into the craft, production, and marketing aspects of the writing/publishing processes. Hanna's work-in-progress is a memoir about the loss of her brother to suicide and her personal history with mental illness. Hanna offers one-on-one coaching for writers struggling to finish their books, is gathering interest for a group program, as well as hosting free, monthly co-writing sessions for Substack subscribers. Learn more about Hanna at hannaetu.com This episode of Creative Alchemy is supported by the audiobook version of my award-winning, Amazon best-selling memoir, Cult, A Love Story. Readers call the book 'compelling' 'gritty' 'intimate' and 'not boring' – which is what an author loves to hear. I narrated the audiobook and if you have a Spotify premium subscription you can listen to the audiobook for free as part of that subscription at alexandraamor.com/spotify . You can listen above, on your favorite podcast app , or watch on YouTube . Notes, links, resources and a full transcript are below. Show notes Working as a book coach with neurodivergent and 'mad' writers Taking ownership of a personal story by writing about it On supporting writers who have challenges with organization Getting to the central idea of what your book stands for Using specific tools to ensure the storytelling in a memoir is captivating Building small habits that support a writing practice How a first draft is often powerful for different reasons than we think Dealing with the challenges of writing about a very emotional subject Resources mentioned in this episode Hanna's Substack piece about beginnings Madwomen in the Attic David Sedaris Mary Karr's memoir Lit Jenny Lawson Transcript of the interview with Hanna Etu Alexandra: Hannah Etu, thank you for coming to Creative Alchemy and welcome. Hanna: Thank you so much for having me. Alexandra: Please tell us a little bit first about your background. Hanna: I am originally from Buffalo, New York. I have an English creative writing and German degree from Canisius University. I have an editorial background. I worked in publishing for a few years for a publishing company in Buffalo, and then when they were bought out by a bigger company, then I went elsewhere. Now I am a certified book coach. I was certified by Author Accelerator in nonfiction and memoir. So now I am helping memoir writers, particularly neurodivergent and mad memoir writers, finish their books. Alexandra: Tell us what mad means, because I was new to that term when we started emailing. Hanna: Sure. Mad in this context is in reference to the Mad movement, so the mental health justice movement. People who may have had adverse mental health experiences, or people who have been negatively affected by the mental health system that may have been involuntarily institutionalized or involuntarily medicated, things like that. That's typically what the MAD moniker refers to. It's comes from the 'mad woman in the attic' idea, from Jane Eyre. That's kind of where that whole thing comes from. It's reclaiming an older term, basically. Alexandra: Got it. What's the reason that you chose to work with writers who are neurodivergent and part of the Mad community. Hanna: There's a whole combination of reasons. I am a lead organizer and regional literacy director for a grassroots feminist mental health literacy organization called Mad Women in the Attic. We advocate for people in the mental health system. And lately, our biggest work has been writing workshops because we've been able to connect with people all around the country. It used to be more localized to Western New York, and now we're doing work with people all around the world. Actually, we've had people in Canada, we've had people in Europe, all over the place. So we've been able to help people write their books, which has been really exciting. So that that is part of the mission. The other part of it is that I'm also neurodivergent. I wasn't diagnosed with anything until I was an adult with anxiety and general depression. And I tend to believe that I have other neurodivergences, but I'm just too high functioning to get a diagnosis. Nobody, none of my practitioners seem terribly interested in diagnosing me because I get through the day. The other the other reason is that both my brothers suffer from mental health issues, and my older brother died by suicide in 2018. So it's a very personal issue, and I really want to connect with people who have had similar experiences to me or similar experiences to the people that I've worked with. It's about a shared experience and validating people and advocating for themselves. It's all about working through our difficulties and finding common bonds. Alexandra: Maybe give us a few examples of how you think writing memoir specifically fulfills those that goal, or helps people to heal and to connect and that kind of thing. Hanna: So with memoir, I think people find it cathartic to write their stories to talk about their traumatic experiences. I think it can be painful. I know personally it can be hard to write about difficult experiences, but I think people find it also find it empowering. In a way they're taking ownership of their story and their writing. They're taking ownership of the narrative, where the narrative has previously been written for them where they may have been in a place where somebody was making the decisions for them and telling a different story about who they are, and they're now able to reclaim that. So I think that's a big part of why a lot of people choose to write memoir. Alexandra: I think that's so true. I was talking to somebody else the other day, and we phrased it in a slightly different way, but I think we were aiming at the same thing. Sometimes it's the first time that someone can tell the truth about their experience, and more specifically, their own truth about their experience. And so that's exactly what you're talking about. That we get to take ownership of the narrative. Hanna: Yeah, exactly. Alexandra: You mentioned that it's a difficult experience, which it is. What are some of the challenges or hurdles that you that your writers encounter when they begin this path? Hanna: There are the difficulties of writing about a traumatic experience and re-experiencing that and having to go through that again. There's also the kind of experience, the kind of writing difficulties that neurodivergent writers have in general. I've noticed a lot of these writers have difficulties with organization, and this isn't like I can't say that this is typical to everyone. Like everybody has their own individual experience, but I have noticed that many writers have expressed that they have a hard time keeping organized, keeping the writing organized, keeping a structure, keeping a regular practice-that's something that a lot of the writers in this community struggle with. I think a lot of writers, going back to the organization, they also have a hard time building a structure around their narrative because memoir is such a broad topic. Figuring out where to start, where to end, when to know what is the end, and and often these aren't positive experiences. These aren't usually positive experiences, and they're trying to end. I mean, you try to end the book on as positive a note as you can, and I think a lot of people have a hard time knowing when is it done? Is it done yesterday? Is it done a couple years ago? Like when? What period of time am I covering? And what is my mission? What is the objective? So there's a lot of different issues that they deal with. Alexandra: That's such a good point about wrapping up a book because when it's a memoir, it's about your life and your life isn't over yet as you're writing. So this may be an unfair question: Are there any tips that you have for finding a good place to end a memoir? Hanna: It's funny because I've been wanting to write a Substack post about this and want to dig into some of my favorite memoirs. I think I would recommend reading a lot of memoir, especially by writers that you admire and writers who are writing in a similar subject matter, but particularly memoir writers, of course. I think seeing kind of comparing those. I did this with beginnings. I did a Substack post on beginnings. Now, of course, I'll have to be held to that. But I kind of analyze. I was like, this is really good because they get right into the action. They don't give us extra exposition. They make us care. Right off the bat. Now I want to kind of do the same thing for endings. How did they make us feel like we bookended this book with the end of the person's arc. There has to be some kind of development. Like obviously your character development, you're not a fictional character. Like you're going to develop as to who you are now, so you're not making anything up if you're a good writer. But in terms of any other techniques that I would recommend, I'm also liking the idea of writing several versions, and it might feel tedious to write multiple endings, but to force yourself to try different, try them on, and see how they fit. I think it's important to focus on where you are as a person, where you're trying to show us that you've gotten by the end of the book, and that's really where we should sit by the end of a memoir. Alexandra: Nice, yes, and very much like fiction, the main character who is us, that's writing the memoir, is going to go through some sort of arc. I guess it's a matter of finding the closure place for that arc Hanna: Yeah. Even if it's not necessarily the happiest ending. Like the writing itself is a reflection for the writer. The writing itself is a reflection on that experience. So, I think even in the process of writing it, you're finding new things about yourself and about that experience. So, it's a hard thing to to think about at the beginning, but it is something important to think about at the beginning of the process and at the end of the process of writing your first draft. Alexandra: Right. A bit of a north star, I guess, to point to you know to write toward if you've thought about where you want it to end up, And then for organization is such a good point. I use a piece of software called Scrivener, which is really helpful for organization because on the left hand side of the screen, what you see is a list of all the chapters that you've written, or you can break it into scenes or whatever you want. What other sorts of organization tips do you have for your writers? Hanna: That sounds great. I think I should try it. In my book coaching certification, we were trained on Jenny Nash's blueprint for a book, and so that has been my north star in terms of organization. I'm working on adapting my own version because I want to add some elements specific to neurodivergent writers. I use the blueprint in my coaching process, but I also use some what's the word I'm looking for? I use some surveying to figure out what every individual writer's style is, what their schedule is, what their needs are, because I think that that's just as important as knowing what their book is about if we're going to work together. But getting off topic, the blueprint is basically it's a set of questions, and eventually you get to an outline, and you're talking about you're digging into the deeper questions about why you're writing the book, and what your book really stands for. What you're trying to say? It's interesting because I don't know if everyone really sits down and thinks about that when they're going to write a memoir. What am I really trying to say with this? Am I just trying to write my story? Which is okay if you just want to write your book and you just want to self-publish it, which is fine, which is great. If you're looking to try to get it to a trade audience, you want there to be some central objective. The blueprint prepares you for the mindset of preparing your book for the literary marketplace. With the memoir blueprint there's an impact outline, where you go through and you break down each scene and what happens in each scene and how it's connected to the one before, and basically you're justifying to yourself and to your coach if you're doing it with a coach why each scene is where it is. Which is very tedious, but it's really enlightening too. Alexandra: That sounds great because it's so important that every scene, every chapter serves a purpose. It serves the narrative in some way. When we're telling a personal story, I know this from personal experience, we can kind of get out there and get lost in the weeds a bit, and think that every detail is important, and every bit of the timeline matters, and every little event that happened is important to include in the story. So that this really speaks to me as a way to narrow our focus and really make sure that yeah that we stay focused on what what matters. Hanna: Exactly. Alexandra: That sounds like a great tool. So you use that tool with your clients to help them to do that. Hanna: Yes. I'm working on adding elements specifically for neurodivergent writers because it is a lot of work upfront. Some coaches will do it in segments. Some coaches will send it to the writer all at once. I'm also thinking about the ways in which I can customize each coaching process for the writer, because everybody works in different ways, and especially neurodivergent writers are wired differently. And some people they can say, “Okay, I'll write an hour a week.” But some people it's like you write in a two-hour burst, and then you don't write for another two months. So that's something that we always have to keep in mind, and as as as a coach for people who with with differently wired brains. Alexandra: Exactly. And you did talk about time as part of what a writer has to organize. I don't know if this is a fair question either, but do you have any tips for people to help them to organize their time? Everybody is so individual with what works for them in terms of writing, as you just said. Some people write in bursts. Some people are like to write every day, just a tiny little bit if they can. What are your thoughts on that sort of organization? Hanna: In terms of writing practice, or in terms of planning the timeline of the book? Alexandra: In terms of writing practice. Getting your bum in your chair. Hanna: I like setting a particular goal. During the pandemic when I could write all the time, I set a goal of 30 minutes a day. Just set a timer, stopped at 30 minutes, whether or not I wanted to keep writing. So then I knew what I was going to write the next day when I sat down. I'm really into the idea of setting a regular time for it, whether it's once a month, once a week, a little bit a day. I'm very much into building small habits. I really like that. I know it doesn't always work for people. My other tip, which is less related to time, but I've been really into body doubling for writers and hopping on Zoom with other writers, and writing for like an hour and a half. So that's something I've been doing as well. I have one once a month, and now I know I'm going to work on my book once a month. Alexandra: Nice, and so it's a group of writers in a Zoom room, and and you're just you're all with your heads down writing. Okay, so it's like accountability. You have to show up. It's like a meeting. Hanna: Exactly. Alexandra: Nice. Hanna: That's my my new favorite way of of maintaining a practice is if you have a body doubling group whether once a week, every other week, twice a week or whatever that really gets your butt in the chair because you know other people are going to be there. Alexandra: That's amazing. That's a great idea. Do you find sometimes with clients who are writing a memoir that one of the things they're looking for is permission to tell their story? Hanna: Yes, almost all the time. And especially with mad writers, because they're dealing with a lot of stigma. I hear them saying so often, “Is anybody going to care about this? Is anybody going to read this?” And these writers are brilliant, they write the most brilliant stories. I'm sitting here thinking, this has to be in the world. You have to publish this. What do you mean? Would anyone care? I care. You've got to publish this for me. I feel like a lot of people come to me and they're like, is this even worth? Is this even worth writing? Will anybody be interested in it? I think that's a very valid fear to have in the memoir writing space now because of how competitive the genre is and how saturated we can be with memoir. The more popular memoirs tend to be people who are either established memoir writers or celebrities, famous people, along those lines, historically relevant people. But I never want to discourage somebody from writing their story. I'm going to tell them what I think they're writing, and if I think they're on the right track. But I'm not going to sugarcoat that feedback on the writing, but I think people will care, especially in these stories of people who have been stigmatized. I think that there's not enough of those stories out there, and I think people would really appreciate to have more of that in the world. Just to feel seen, people who are not brave enough to tell their stories or talk about how they're feeling and the differences that they're noticing about themselves, to see somebody else feels the way that they do, like that is so important. Alexandra: I absolutely agree. To have an experience reflected back to a person is just so valuable. So incredible and so brave on the part of the writer. I want to bring this up because I had never seen this quote from Terry Pratchett. You posted it on Instagram a little while ago that I love so much. The quote is: “The first draft is you telling yourself the story.” Why did that quote resonate with you, and what do you think it says? Hanna: I really like that because I think that writers underestimate the power of the first draft. I think that we tend to think, okay, first draft, give it a little edit, or maybe overestimate is the better term for it, but write the first draft, give it a little copy edit. It's good to go. But the first draft is so powerful for a different reason. It''s important because it tells us exactly how, in terms of memoir writers, but also for fiction writers, how we see the story, how in our original voice, how we picture it. What so many writers get wrong is that the writing becomes stronger through revision and revision and revision. I think if more writers knew how much revision their books would really need, they probably wouldn't have started writing their books in the first place. I think that's why that quote really resonated with me because I think that the first draft is so important and so personal that it's very much for the writer, for you to process your story and and to just tell it, just get everything out unfiltered. Especially with a memoir when you could be writing about people that you may eventually not want to write about anymore, or people that need to be concealed in some way for the purposes of privacy. It's always better to write everything raw, unfiltered, and then go back and pare it down, edit it down, so that it's appropriate for publishing. So the first draft is always something that I think really is meant for the writer, whereas a second draft is where you start going. All right, let's talk to a developmental editor or a beta reader. I think we have to spend more time with our first draft. Alexandra: I love all that. My experience has been the same; that it's so true and often you know I mean there's so much in there it's so rich we don't know what we think sometimes until we've written it down. Or we don't know the impact that an experience has had until we get quiet and write it down. I know for me, with my memoir, I learned stuff about the cult that I was in by trying to explain it to the reader. So that's a slightly different topic than a first draft, but it did happen in the first draft where I would realize the cult leader did this so that six months later she could do this other thing over here. I didn't see it at the time when I was in the group, but trying to explain it enabled me to see what had happened. I imagine that's true for anybody who's writing down an experience that they've had. Hanna: I think with the benefit of hindsight, we start to reflect on people's motives and what people were thinking, or when we write about past experiences with what we know now about those people and start to put the puzzle pieces together, and it's very interesting what you find, but you won't necessarily find it unless you write it down. That's just the way the human brain works. Alexandra: One of the things you mentioned at the top of the show was that you are sadly a survivor of suicide. You lost a brother to that, and when we were emailing back and forth, you mentioned that you hadn't written your memoir about that yet. I think it might be valuable for our listeners to hear about your thoughts about that potential book and the issues that you're facing finding time to write. You've addressed that a little bit already with the the Zoom group. You called it body doubling. I'd never heard that before. Tell us a little bit about your thoughts about what you've encountered thinking about writing that book. Hanna: I've written about 30,000 words. I wrote a lot during the pandemic. I was writing, as I said, I think I got to like a 30 minute a day writing practice, and I was in one of the writing workshops. I was trying to have something to read and share every week. So that really pushed me. The people pleaser in me really pushed me to to have something to write. You get to a certain point where – I think it was two or three years after I lost my brother that I started writing about it, and that was still very raw, and I think I got to a point where I realized that there was still a lot of healing that I needed to do. I don't think that's why I stepped back from writing it. I definitely stepped back from writing it because I was working on my book coaching business, and I have a lot of other hobbies and activities that I do, and I have just a lot of going on in my life at the time, and so I stopped making the time for it. But I definitely hit a wall creatively with it at a certain point where I hadn't done the deep thinking that you're supposed to do when you sit down. I had just written. I had just been writing. I wrote everything that happened from the day that my brother died, to his funeral, and through that. I wrote all of the events that went from there to there, and then started digging into my mental health history, and digging into his mental health history, and my family's history with mental health. I began realizing I had just all these moving parts, and I had no idea where everything should go, where the timeline should be. I had just taken all the rules that I so preach to writers, and just broken all of them. I've recently gotten back into it with the co-writing with the body doubling, which has been so valuable, and I've gone back and I started doing the blueprint, which I've started before, but I've gone back into it. That has been so valuable because it's doing what we talked about with the first draft, where you're just writing things out and you're writing things out, and I started writing again. Why am I writing this book? Because I just feel called to it, like losing losing someone to suicide, especially someone who was. I was 25. He was 27 at the time. Their life is so short, and he was so creative, so artistic. He was a filmmaker. He was also a writer, an artist. He painted. He made clay figures and different clay things. He's a sculptor. I think that I wanted my my original mission with it was like there was so much left unfinished in his life where he was supposed to reach a certain point. He was supposed to, I don't know, become a famous filmmaker or he was supposed to go on to direct a movie, whatever. I had this vision of what I thought his life should become, and now I'm going to write a book to tell everybody else about this person because I want him to live on in the ways that I remember him. Which of course is also another layered part of it, in that my memory of him isn't everyone else's memory of him, isn't how he remembered himself. And there are things that you learn after the fact. It's been very complicated to write about and figure out exactly what I'm doing. But I actually was writing about it yesterday; just free writing and trying to figure out why I'm doing this, why I'm doing this, what is the point, what does my book stand for, because it has to stand for something. I started to really have more epiphanies than I had had in a while, so I'm very excited. It's making me more motivated to get writing and have a better structure, a beginning, middle, and an end. I can talk about this forever. Alexandra: This is great. Thank you for your vulnerability. I really appreciate it. Hanna: I think for a while, I was stuck because I also didn't know how it was going to end. I didn't know what the ending would be, and I thought the ending should be me in a place where I have dealt with my grief, or I have overcome my grief, or moved forward with it. And that's not really how grief works. But I couldn't figure out what version of me am I stopping this book at? For so many years after my brother died, I was in a relationship that was very toxic, and so I was not the best version of myself. And now that that is no longer part of my life, I'm finally realizing that I'm a more skilled person. It actually has allowed me to grieve more, and that's been incredibly helpful, and really brought me to a place where I can say I feel like I'm starting to see the resolution. I'm starting to see the ending, which is a really good feeling. So those are the challenges that I've been having around it, but it is getting better. Alexandra: Thank you so much for all of that. You brought up so many important points. I think, or special points, one of them being that it does feel sometimes like books have a gestation period, and sometimes we can't force it, just like giving birth. You can't make it happen necessarily, and having patience with ourselves as things are going on, and the book feels like it's just kind of sitting there, that can be a challenge in and of itself. Hanna: Yes,I think I needed to wait and see what the book was going to be because I was still living it, which so many of us are. Alexandra: Absolutely. And you bring up the point about grief too, and how it's not linear at all, and the importance of taking care of yourself, both just as a human being, but also as a writer. I just think it's so important to put a pin in that and notice that we can't ignore those things., especially when we're writing about something so close to our hearts. Hanna: Yes. Alexandra: We wish you all the best with that book. Please let me know when it comes out, and I'll make a mention of it for sure. Hanna: Wonderful, thank you. Yeah, I will. Alexandra: As we start to wrap up here, I wanted to ask you, what are some of your favorite memoirs? Hanna: I got into memoir by reading David Sedaris, so I love everything by David Sedaris. But in terms of really deep, like I love Mary Carr Lit is one of my absolute favorites. Just one of those where I felt like I could just soak up every page. I love everything she writes. I like Sloane Crosley, who wrote recently a book called Grief Is for People. It was about losing her best friend by suicide in the last few years. I really liked that, and I tend to really connect with humour writers who write about mental health. Jenny Lawson, her name is escaping me now. It'll come to me later. Alexandra: Jenny Lawson. I haven't read any of her books, but I've seen people mention them, and her titles alone are hilarious. I'm trying to think of one now. I'll link to them in the show notes, but yeah, they're very funny. Hanna: I think I've read every book she's written. She recently did a book, How To Be Okay When Everything Is Not Okay, and it was a little less memoir, but more about staying creative when times are tough, and that really that was a really good book. She got really serious when she needed to, but also very silly when the occasion warranted it. Alexandra: Oh, that's great. All right. Tell us, Hannah, where we can find out more about you and your work. Hanna: You can find me at hannetu.com. That's Hanna with no H on the end, and you can find me on Substack. You can find me on Instagram, Hannah Etu Book Coach, or on Facebook, Hannah Etu Book Coach. Alexandra: Great. Okay. I'm going to link to all those things, but also specifically to your series on beginnings in Substack because you mentioned that because I think that would be really helpful for people. Hanna: I'll make sure it's up there if it's not. So I know I wrote it. We'll have to make sure it's on the substack. Alexandra: Okay. Great. All right. Well, thank you again so much for being with me here today. I really appreciate it. Hanna: You're welcome. Thank you so much for having me. Alexandra: My pleasure. episodes.title: Telling Our Truth in Writing with Bella Mahaya Carter
episodes.description: Bella Mahaya Carter is an experienced writer and writing teacher. In this episode she shares how she used the support of an editor to meet that small, 1000 words per month goal as a way to break the enormous task of writing a memoir into small, achievable steps. In the introduction, inspired by this interview, I talk about thinking outside the box when we are looking for support for our creative projects. And I talk about a subject very close to my heart; the idea that writing and journaling can sometimes be the first time a cult survivor, or survivor of other trauma, tells the truth about their experience. And how powerful that can be. This episode of Creative Alchemy is supported by the Creative Alchemy journaling handbook. This free ebook guides cult and other trauma survivors into the healthy and healing practice of journaling. With a gentle hand and relying on her decades of writing experience, cult survivor Alexandra Amor encourages readers to develop a journaling practice as part of their healing path. Click here to get your complimentary copy. Bella Mahaya Carter is the award-winning author of three books including Where Do You Hang Your Hammock: Finding Peace of Mind While You Write, Publish, and Promote Your Book, a guide for writers. She is currently completing Ripe: A Memoir of the Lives We Carry, which explores intergenerational trauma, creativity, motherhood, and the stories we inherit—and choose to transform. Her writing has appeared in dozens of literary journals, and her last two books have received five book awards. Bella is the founder of Write Where You Are writing circles and has been teaching and coaching writers for more than twenty years. Her mission is to help writers explore what they're carrying so they can write and live with greater truth, agency, and freedom. Learn more about Bella at BellaMahayaCarter.com You can listen above, on your favorite podcast app , or watch on YouTube . Notes, links, resources and a full transcript are below. Show Notes: Beginning as a dancer and moving into filmmaking and then writing Discovering Shakespeare in college and falling in love with the musicality of his writing Starting to write a book about family secrets several decades ago Writing about what we inherit from family and what we choose to carry forward Finding the question at the heart of a memoir Learning to write in micro and flash non-fiction Using a monthly editorial deadline to support getting a book written What a story teaches us as we write it How it's never too late to begin Using journaling to access the wise parts of ourselves How 'no' can often just mean 'not yet' Why being seen and recognized is an inside job Why we can begin a creative project before you feel ready Find the thing that will help you get out of your own way Resources Mentioned in this Episode Bella's writing circles, Write Where You Are Bella's Substack, Flying Lessons for Writers Creative Alchemy journaling handbook Transcript of Interview Alexandra: Bella Mahaya Carter, welcome to Creative Alchemy. Bella: Thank you. It's great to be here. Alexandra: Great to have you here. Give us a little bit about your background, Bella. Maybe your education and your writing background. Bella: Okay, I'll start with my education. My post-secondary school education started at the Juilliard School. I was a dancer, and I had a back injury and had to stop dancing, and went to college at Scripps College in Claremont, California, which is a small liberal arts college for women. After that, I actually went to film school at USC, the School of Cinematic Arts, and I got a master of fine arts degree in filmmaking with an emphasis in screenwriting. I taught in the screenwriting department as a teaching assistant. 10 years went by, and I did a lot of writing, and then I went back to school for another master's degree in spiritual psychology, and that really changed my life. That work, so that's my educational. I went to the University of Santa Monica in Santa Monica, so that's my educational background. My writing background is-I really didn't know I was a writer until when I went to Scripps College. Well, I didn't even know I was a writer then. I was a dancer, and I wasn't a great reader. I think I had some maybe dyslexia or some kind of neurodivergency, so I wasn't a reader as a kid, which just makes me so sad even now to this day. But I discovered Shakespeare in college, and I thought how could somebody write plays in poetry, and I just loved it. I used to listen to the old records while reading my Pelican Shakespeare in the library for hours. I could lose myself just listening to the language and the poetry, and I knew that I loved it. And then I took another class with that same teacher on contemporary women writers, and just loved it, loved it, loved it. I didn't know I was a writer yet. I went to film school because I thought, well, my background is dance, and now I'm interested in literature. And I thought, well, maybe combining dance and literature, I could find my way through through movie making. And I was in Los Angeles, but what I discovered in film school, I was one of maybe five women in the program. It was very it was a very male dominated environment, and I thought also I don't really like Hollywood that much. So around that time, I stumbled into a creative writing workshop, and I remember that the teacher he was teaching a UCLA extension class. His name was Jack Grapes, and he wrote this incredible poem about menstruation. And he read it, and I thought to myself, any man who could write about menstruation in that way is someone I think I would like to study with. And I studied with Jack for five years, and that was just the beginning of many many years of writing. Haven't stopped writing since. Alexandra: Nice. Oh, that's great. And you're the author of several books, including a memoir called Raw about. Oh, my mind is going blank. Anxiety. Bella: Yeah, my three books are right behind me. Secrets of My Sex, is a collection of poems, and there's Raw, My Journey from Anxiety to Joy. And there's Where Do you Hang Your Hammock? Finding peace of mind while you write, publish, and promote your book. Alexandra: Right, and we're going to come back to your writing classes and that kind of thing in just a minute. But I want to start with the project you've been working on for the last couple of years, so tell us about that. Bella: You mean my whole life? Alexandra: Yes, yes, exactly. Tell us about that project. Start wherever you want. Bella: My current project is called Ripe: A Memoir of the Lives We Carry, and I kind of officially started writing it over 35 years ago, and but really there were whispers of family secrets and the rupture that had happened in our family. My mom was a great researcher, and she always would whisper the family, some of the family stories to me. Not all of them, the rest of them took me years to learn. But this seed was always planted. My grandfather was a poet and a journalist, so I think it was kind of in my blood. But I wrote this 500-page mess of a manuscript 35 years ago. Didn't know what to do with it, so I put it away in my file cabinet. And at around that time, I was also thinking about becoming a mother. And really, what the book is about, it's a memoir about what we inherit and what we choose to carry forward. I think the question that is at the heart of the memoir for me was, how do I create life without surrendering my own or perpetuating inherited pain? And though I didn't have the writing skills or the maturity, or the experience, and many other things to to write that that project in my 30s. I discovered about four years ago that I was revisiting that project. I had discovered the 100 word story format, fell in love with concise forms and real and started mining two manuscripts. I had one was a manuscript about my high risk pregnancy, the other was a manuscript about the ancestor story, and I just started plucking from those manuscripts. And then after about two years of doing that, I thought I'm going to ask my publisher at She Writes Press, if she thinks this is a viable way to approach a memoir. Because it was in micro and flash stories, so the stories could be anywhere from 50 words to 1000 words. And when I showed it to her, she loved it. She said, “I think this is the future of memoir because we have shorter attention spans. I think that this hybrid form is going to be very, very popular.” So that was in May of 2024, and I'm almost done. Out of the 200 stories, I think I have about eight left to write. Alexandra: And it sounds like you had a plan, if you know how many stories are left. What's that based on? Bella: Well, actually, I just figured that out today. Alexandra: Oh, okay. Bella: I had a rough idea of what material I needed to cover at the end, and I am at the beginning of every month. So at the end of every month, I send my editor at least a minimum of 1000 words, and then I start fresh on the next journey, the next chapter series of chapters. At the beginning of the month, I'm always like, I'm never going to make my deadline. I don't know how I'm going to do this, but because what happens is I dig into archives. I have family, archives. Last month, I read 32 letters written by my great-grandmother in 1961, and I had to create one composite letter conveying her experience, like a literary piece, rather than just using her letters. This month, the end of the story is my experience with the repair of the family, and so I actually read yesterday my journal from when I was in Italy in 1994 with my mother, meeting the family and discovering my great-great-grandfather's diary and other primary source materials. So it wasn't until this morning, after I read my journal from that trip, and then I was writing in my journal that the structure for the things that I want to cover emerged. And so just today I realized, oh, I have about eight more stories left. Alexandra: Amazing. So, for our listeners, we should explain this is such a unique project in my mind because you have all this archival material. Tell our listeners a little bit about your great-grandmother's letters. Bella: What happened was in 1918, my great grandfather, who was a doctor, he lived in New Haven, Connecticut. He got the family servant pregnant, and performed an illegal abortion on her, and was arrested, jumped bail, and left like he went to New York and disappeared because he was fugitive. And then various things happened. His wife divorced him, this was an Italian Catholic family, so divorce was pretty much unheard of and shameful, and people whispered. And after the divorce was granted my grandfather, whose custody had been awarded to my great-grandmother, and very soon after he kidnapped his son, returned to Italy because he was from Italy, and when the authorities and when the authorities caught up with him in Italy. He escaped to Argentina, where he raised his son. They stayed there for 10 years, on the lam, they were hiding from the law, and it just goes on and on. I thought I was writing the story of the rupture that occurred in our family, but as I started reading letters from my mother, my grandmother, my grandmother's brother, my great grandfather. Though nobody spoke about what went on, everybody felt the need to write their version of it for posterity. What I've learned over the last maybe eight months is that I'm writing a story not only of rupture, but of repair, because only half the story is the rupture. The other half the story is how the family found its way back together Alexandra: Wow! You mentioned there that one of themes of the book is whether or not we carry trauma forward. Bella: Well, this is why you know I had originally in my 30s written two books. One was a family story. One was my pregnancy story, and it was really an exploration of you know trying to like how do I maintain my identity as a person, as a creative artist, and then also be a mom. I didn't know how to do that. I didn't see that model well. I shouldn't say I didn't see it modeled. I did see it modeled, but I was really worried about it. I was like, “How am I going to do that? And how am I going to not pass on the pain that I felt, even though I couldn't really at that time articulate what the pain was. I just knew it was painful to be alive, and do I really want my child to experience that? It wasn't until a few years ago that when I started plucking stories from both manuscripts that I realized, oh wow, this should be a braided narrative. These two books, and I had written like I was a very inexperienced writer, so the manuscripts were a mess. They were kitchen sinks. They had some overlapping stories and stuff. So I just realized, oh, I could braid these two narratives, like because they're commenting on each other. One is the story of being afraid to get pregnant, and then finally deciding to get pregnant, and then realizing, and for three years I couldn't get pregnant, and then finally getting pregnant and having the doctor call it a geriatric pregnancy because I was 36. Then so much of it was about claiming agency over my own life and my own experience because four months, five months into the pregnancy, I just felt like I was like a lamb being led to the slaughter. I felt like I had no choice about how things were done, and I thought, you know what? I want to have a natural childbirth. I don't want I don't want this. And but unfortunately, my insurance company said you have a pre-existing condition, pregnancy. You can't do that, but I did do it. I did do it, and I practiced throughout the pregnancy, having some agency over that experience while I was flashing back to the ancestral story as it was unfolding. Alexandra: Amazing, and so tell us a little bit about the challenges you've encountered, and I think you've touched on this already. You tried writing the book 35 years ago. That was maybe one challenge. What have the others been? Bella: Oh, there have been so many challenges. I think the biggest challenge was me, because I just always felt like I wasn't good enough. And one component of the book that I haven't mentioned is the repercussions that my great-grandmother's experience had on my parents' lives, or had on these succeeding generations. My grandmother also had a very turbulent relationship. My mother was molested by her father when she was a child. My mother married a man who was abusive. There were just ripples of this problem that went all the way down through the generations up until my generation. Part of what I learned as a small child, who was beaten sometimes, was I'm bad, and I think I learned very early on to to be an excellent people pleaser, and to not really listen to myself so much as to just pay attention, to read the room, figure out what you need to do, to so that the shit doesn't hit the fan. I think that kind of spilled into my writing with questions like, “Who do you think you are? What makes you think you can be a writer?” I think that was the hardest thing, and the reason why I said my U.S.M. education in spiritual psychology was the most profound for me was, I mean, it was all profound, but that was particularly profound. I entered that at the age of 40 something, early 40s, thinking that I had failed, that my life was a failure because I had five manuscripts in my file cabinet that hadn't gone anywhere. I just thought, wow! Like, if I don't, I'm not sure what I. I remember when I had to stop dancing, and my identity was so tied up with being a dancer. It was like, well, if I'm not a dancer, who am I? And it took me some years, and then I glommed onto this idea that I'm a writer. But I think what I learned in that program is that we are not what we do. We are spiritual beings having a human experience, and there's no such thing as failure. There are only opportunities for growth. Alexandra: Oh, nicely said. I imagine that feelings come up as you're reading this archival material that you've got. Is there some processing that goes on? Bella: Absolutely. It's funny because just today I had a little moment with my husband, a little moment of conflict as I mentioned something about the pain. His immediate response was, oh, but there was lots of love too, and I said no, no, no, you don't understand. We have to make space for the pain. We have to allow it. We have to acknowledge the pain. Part of the interesting thing about the story is that it wasn't spoken. No one talked about it. It wasn't acknowledged. The pain, the harm that was done was not acknowledged, so it's not like I want to harp on the pain because it was a ton of creativity and love and music and joy, but to not acknowledge the pain perpetuates it. Alexandra: Have you specifically ever bumped into things like has it brought up big feelings for you? Bella: I have all sorts of ways of dealing with big feelings. I mean, I work in my journal, and I I hesitate to say I work in my journal. I would rather say I listen in my journal, and the force that I listen to that I call my wise self. When I show up there, I get guidance from a source that is greater than me. That is not the little complaining, worried person that I can be. It's an eternal presence that resides within us all. I believe. I also move. I'm still a dancer, even though I don't dance in that way. I like to move. I like to put on music. I like to move my body and let my body. I just listen with my body, and then I'll just move. I'll try to move energy and release stuff that's in my body that I can feel in my body. And I practice yoga, and I do Reiki, and I do massages. Like I have a you know practices that I engage in regularly to help move them. Alexandra: Nice. And so going back to this, the wise self that you talk to in your journal, can you take us through what that looks like? What do you do to access that part of yourself? Bella: I just sit down with my journal. I just show up, and then I just start complaining, and then eventually the wise self shows up. It doesn't take long, and then the wise self will start speaking in the second person. I've been complaining in the first person, and the wise person will say, “Bella, you just relax, slow down. It's okay. Like give yourself a break. You don't have to be perfect. Look at what you've been dealing with. You've been traveling with your mother in Italy, and she can be very challenging sometimes. And you know, I'm sure you're just as challenging to her. You know, just like chill.” I'll realize, oh yeah, I'm reminded. And then, and if I have questions, I'll ask questions. For a long time, I did left-handed writing because I was forced to slow down when I wrote with my left hand, non-dominant handwriting, because that way I was forced to slow down and listen. But I ask a lot of questions and I just try to listen and it's just there always for all of us. But I think most of us don't know that it's there. We don't know that we can access this wisdom within, and that it is there, and it does guide us, and it doesn't care about the things that we think are such big deals in our lives. I didn't get what I wanted. It's something much larger. And knowing that's there just means that I'm kind of okay no matter what. Alexandra: I love that. While writing this big project, this family history interwoven with your pregnancy: Have you ever had any moments where you hit the wall, didn't know where to go or what to do next? Bella: Yeah, I mean, when I wrote the pregnancy book? Oh my gosh, I was so naive. I can remember I actually sent it out to some agents, just the pregnancy book, and I mean, it was a first draft. It wasn't even a first draft. I remember it got returned to me, and it would sit on my step, and I would walk in my gate, and I would be like, “I hope nobody sees this. I hope nobody knows that I'm a failed writer.” I felt so much shame around it, but I didn't have any idea that there were certain prerequisites that I had to fulfill in order to complete a project of this scope. And so I thought I was failing, failing, failing, but in fact, when I read, I actually have it right here on my desk. This was my journal from when I was in Italy. It says summer 1994. I had made a paper collage over it, and as I was reading yesterday, the paper just was it's so old it was just peeling off. So I just had to peel it all off and took pictures of it. It wasn't, “No, you're not good enough.” It was, “Not yet”, right? Not yet. And it's and the number of not yets. Like I didn't know they were not yets. I just thought it was no, no, no. You suck. You're not good enough. Why are you trying? I didn't know that. I mean, I knew I was on my path, but I kind of hoped that I could gain some recognition or be seen. What I realized is being seen and getting recognition, it's an inside job, because you never know where your writing is going to go. And there's like I don't know a million books, more than a million books published every day in America. My joy right now is working on this project, and I almost don't want it to end because I know what comes next. I know then it's okay, publishing decisions and marketing and all that publicity, and I'm loving the writing so much. I'm loving the discovery, and I'm also feeling like I got to be with my mom in Rome in 1948, and my grandmother in 1950. I feel like I'm knowing parts of my ancestors that I never knew before, and so I feel just so rich. That's the reason. I mean, that's substantial. I don't think anything that could happen after I'm done writing this could be as profound as that. That's the gift. Alexandra: I was just going to say, that is such a gift. That's amazing. One of the things that I really admire about you because we're. For the listeners, we're in a mastermind group together, and we have been for six or seven years, maybe now at this point. Is that how you have held this project so lightly? It seems to me, and have let it evolve as it wanted to. I guess one of the things that I saw was you mentioned writing in the micro and flash fiction, and I at the time I thought Bella: It's nonfiction. Alexandra: Sorry nonfiction. You started to learn about that format, and then and then realized that was the direction that you wanted to take for the book. And this question might be a little bit vague: Can you talk about the balance between having a clear vision for a project and also letting it evolve if it wants to. Bella: Here's what I've learned about. I love this question, by the way. Here's what I've learned: is that you must begin before you feel ready. Alexandra: Ah, yes. Bella: Every month for the last two, well, maybe the whole time I've been working with my editor, which is since 2024. No, 2022. So it's been four years I've been working on this with her. Every time at the beginning of a new month, when I go back to my archives and I'm like, I have a general idea where, like just today, I didn't know. I didn't have the outline. I didn't have a clear outline to the end of the ancestral story. I wrote the pregnancy story some time ago. I've been working on the ancestral story, and then when it's done, I'll weave them. But what I've learned is that the thing about the creative process is that you just have to have faith that even though you don't know where you're going or you just have a hazy glimmer of where you might be going, you have to do it anyway. You have to just start. I always think of that great E. L. Doctorow quote: “writing a novel is like driving on a mountain road at night. You can only see as far as your headlights illuminate.” Same thing with writing. You just look at what's right in front of you. What's the next thing that you need to do? For me yesterday, I wasn't sure what the next thing was. I was like, oh, the next thing is read your journal from Italy in 1994, and then I did that, and I was like, oh my god! And then it was like, what's the next thing? I got to write about this in my journal. I didn't know this morning when I wrote in my journal that the outline for the rest of the ancestral story would emerge, I had no idea. So I never know, really. Even when I work with outlines, like for Raw, My Journey from Anxiety to Joy, I remember when I first started that project, my editor wanted me to outline it, and I thought, okay, I was pretty clear. Raw is divided into three sections: body, mind, and spirit. I pretty much knew the body story and I knew the mind story. But what I didn't know was that I hadn't yet lived the spirit story. That spiritual stuff was going to come and hit the fan while I was working, so I fudged it in the outline, and I did the best I could. And then, as I was writing, actually in the middle of that project, we had five family deaths in three years, and I was the executor of my mom's estate, and it was contentious. I developed an anxiety disorder, and I was scared to leave my house. I really didn't know that I had kind of been suffering with the low-grade anxiety for most of my life until it exploded and became a full-on disorder that made me dysfunctional. In that time, I also had some mystical experiences that showed me who I really am and what really matters. Once I lived through that, I completely revised my outline for the last section of the book. People say, are you a plotter or a panster? Do you plot an outline or do you just fly by the seat of your pants? And I would say that I do both. I really love structure, but I also like to wander, and I think both for me, my writing is served both by wandering and also figuring out what the structure is. And usually, after a while, the structure just emerges, like it did this morning when I was working in my journal. Alexandra: So well said, and I love that. Begin almost before you're ready. Bella: Just begin before you're ready. Alexandra: Yes, exactly. Bella: And just have faith. Just trust the process. I tell this to my students all the time. Whatever the big trick is to get out of your own way, so that what wants to come through you is free to come through you. That's the trick, and to not worry so much about what it is because eventually it will announce itself. This project announced itself two years ago when I realized, huh, I've been pulling stories from both of these manuscripts. I wonder if I could combine these these two manuscripts and make a one one manuscript instead of like two horribly long kitchen sink manuscripts that meander in every which direction. What if I just plucked and chiseled and polished each story presented it that way? It's a mosaic, and it's beautiful because each story stands on its own and has its own narrative. But then it's also part of a larger story. Alexandra: I think this project is such a good example of the right time and place. 35 years ago, obviously, you weren't the writer that you are now, and you hadn't learned all the things that you've learned now at this point in your life. I think it's so great that we can come back to these things. If it's not the right time now, then it'll be the right time later. Bella: Maybe or maybe not. I'm just reading this book by Elizabeth Jarrett Andrew. I don't know if you know her. She's a wonderful writer. It's called. It's something about. I meant to bring it with me and have it here for the interview, but because I knew I knew it was going to come up because I've been reading it. It's on my mind. She says that it's valuable to write even if you don't want to publish. So even if I hadn't picked up this manuscript, working on it the way I did for a decade, I worked on it for a decade in my 30s. That changed me. That grew me. So even if we don't publish our work, it doesn't make the writing any less valuable. Alexandra: I totally agree. Yes, because as you say, and I believe this too, it's what's happening to us as we're writing it that actually matters. The end result is a nice cherry on top, but what really matters is what happens to us. Bella: At the end of the day, the writing writes us. That's true of dance too. When I dance, the dancing is dancing me. Alexandra: Nice. Oh, that's lovely. So that's a great segue. You are a writing teacher, and you've been doing that for a while. What have you noticed about the healing that takes place with your students when they write? Bella: Okay, well, first let's just break that up into two pieces. Maybe the first piece is I thought you were going to ask me what do you notice in your students because you're a writing teacher. What do you notice in your students, just in a more general way? Because we'll get to the healing. That's part B of the question. Part A of the question is the first thing that I notice is that most people don't recognize their own gifts, and most people engaged in a creative endeavor that involves vulnerability and self-expression, or that involves self-expression which necessitates vulnerability, they need to feel safe. They need to understand that it's a sacred process, and they need to be held and supported and loved. Period. That's the first thing. In terms of growth as a writer, anytime anybody wants critical feedback, they can receive that, but only if they ask for it. And there's all kinds. There's many ways to learn. I personally don't think that heavy criticism is the best way to teach people how to learn how to write. I think people need to feel free and unencumbered and celebrated. So when that happens, I'm segueing to part B. When that happens, people realize that all the things that they thought they couldn't say, they can say. And when that happens, people are starting to connect with the divine eternal wisdom that they have inside of themselves, and that is healing because that divine eternal wisdom knows a lot more than we do, and that's what I mean when I say get out of your own. I help people get out of their own way. Alexandra: What are some ways that you do that? Bella: I do that by setting ground rules, such as when someone's done reading, I'm going to ask the group, “What did you appreciate about what you heard?” You're only allowed to say what you appreciated. You're not allowed to make suggestions for improvement. You're not allowed to say parts that were confusing. You're not allowed to make any helpful comments. You're only allowed to say what you appreciated about what you heard. They're small groups, anywhere from six to eight people in a group, and then usually every person in the group gets a chance to say what they appreciated, and that creates trust in the group. It's not like oh that person didn't speak. No, it's like everybody says what they appreciated, and you can always find something to appreciate, even from the most beginning writer. There's always something to appreciate, so I cultivate in my students an ear for listening for what they appreciate. Then I ask the writer, “Do you have any questions? And then the writer can say, “Oh, you know, did it make sense when I did X, Y, and Z, or was it confusing when I spoke about this, or do you have any suggestions for improving the language?” Alot of times people just say no, I'm good, and that's fine, and they learn from each other, they learn from the conversations, and it's a powerful environment. It's called Write Where You Are, and I've been teaching for over 20 years and have helped hundreds of writers, and many of them have gone on to publish books and become authors and healers and leaders in their communities. I will say this about that work. One time I was having a conversation with this writer. I think this was before I became a writing teacher and coach. I thought I had to wait till I had a book published before I could teach writing. Which now that I look back, I didn't need to do that. I could have still taught writing. I waited longer than I needed to, but this woman said to me, I'll never forget. She said, “You, madam, are a natural born coach”. I remember thinking, “Huh”, and that was years before I became one. I think the reason is I see, I do see the sort of divine spark in everybody that I work with, and unlike writing, which was a the skill, the craft of writing took me my whole life to to to practice and learn. I do have a God given gift, or I don't know if you want to use the word God, but I do have a gift that comes to me from the universe that just I understand what people need. Maybe it's because I did live in that household that was violent and difficult, and in order to stay alive, I had to be really perceptive about what was going on. So, I'm sensitive and intuitive, and I can tell what each person needs, and what each person needs is different from what another person needs, and I just tune into that. This is the reason why I don't write in my writing circles myself. I know the Amherst method says you've got to show your students you're one of them, you're just like them, you're a writer too. But I find that my writer self is too insecure. I can't focus on my writer. I can't show up as my writer self and then also do this thing with where I tune into people and guide them. To me, those are just two different lives. So I don't write with my students. I focus all my attention on their growth and upliftment. Alexandra: I love the point you brought up there that writing is an opportunity to tell the truth. I'm sure you encounter that sometimes it's the first time a person has told the truth about an experience that they've had. Bella: Yeah, and many people have been ghosted. Many people-is that the right word? Ghosted. I feel like that. I'm wondering if that's the right word. Well, it doesn't matter. Many people show up having no idea, even what their truth is. Alexandra: Yes. Even just writing in a journal is an opportunity to tell the truth. Bella: And an opportunity to tell the truth and to connect with the small quiet voice within, which is the voice of wisdom, and many people once they come to the circles, they stay. They stay for a long time. There's one every eight weeks. I have a student who's been with me for 10 years. I have students who've been with me three years, five years. I think people are hungry for the freedom of a of a small supportive community that can hold space for them while they explore whatever it is they need to explore on the page. Alexandra: I'm just having a huge epiphany right now while we're talking about how writing is sometimes the first time a person will slow down enough, and tell the truth, even if it's just to themselves about an experience that they've had. And how valuable that's been in my life and in others' lives that I've seen, and what a gift that you are able to support people to do that. Bella: Yeah, lovely. I feel like actually the gift was given to me, and I think the best kind of gifts are the ones that energetically keep moving. Alexandra: Yes, nicely said. Speaking of your writing circles, tell us where we can find out more about you and your work. Bella: My website is bellamahaya carter.com, and it has my writing there, my publications, my writing circles, coaching information. It's all there. I also write a monthly Substack newsletter called Flying Lessons for Writers, and I try each month to write something that I feel very connected to that I think will inspire other writers to fly both on the page and in their lives, because I am interested very much in writing. I love writing and I love the craft of writing and I love to help people become better writers and I'm constantly trying myself to become a better writer and I'm equally fascinated in becoming as large and authentic a human being as possible, and I'm equally interested in facilitating that process in others through the medium of writing. Alexandra: Great, awesome. I will put links to all those things in the show notes so people can find you and your work. This has been a real pleasure, Bella. Is there anything else you wanted to share before we wrap up? Bella: Ah, let's see. Gosh, this time went fast. I don't think so. I guess I just want to say thank you for having me on your show. I'm excited to watch all of your interviews. Alexandra: Well, thank you so much. I appreciate that. All right. Well, take care, and I will see you soon. Bella: All right. Take care. episodes.title: Art Therapy for Cult Survivors with Natalee Bigger Stockdale
episodes.description: Natalee Bigger Stockdale is a cult survivor and an art therapist. In this episode, Natalee and I talk about the healing power of creative expression for cult survivors, and other survivors of trauma. Among other topics, Natalee points out that when we use visual means of creative expression (painting, drawing, etc.) we bypass the language areas of our brain, which accesses other parts of ourselves that need healing. She also talks about how creative expression is an excellent tool for helping us recover our sense of self after being in a high-demand group. In the introduction, I talk about a recent article that highlights the art therapy being made available to wildfire evacuees in Penticton, British Columbia. This episode of Creative Alchemy is supported by the audiobook version of my award-winning, Amazon best-selling memoir, Cult, A Love Story. Readers call the book 'compelling' 'gritty' 'intimate' and 'not boring' – which is what an author loves to hear. I narrated the audiobook and if you have a Spotify premium subscription you can listen to the audiobook for free as part of that subscription at alexandraamor.com/spotify . Natalee Bigger Stockdale holds a bachelor's degree in studio art and business from the University of Northwestern and a master's degree in clinical mental health counseling and art therapy from Adler Graduate School. She has worked in clinical practice as a Board-Certified Art Therapist (ATR-BC), Licensed Professional Clinical Counselor (LPCC), and is a Board-Certified Neurofeedback provider (BCN-L). Natalee completed a postgraduate certificate in the Psychology of Coercive Control (PgCert) through Salford Univeristy and has relocated to purse doctoral work with Florida State University in the Art Therapy Practice and Research Program, supporting the recovery journey of victims of exploitative persuasion. Self-portrait by Natalee Bigger Stockdale Connect with Natalee at LinkedIn . You can listen above, on your favorite podcast app , or watch on YouTube . Notes, links, resources and a full transcript are below. Show Notes Discovering art therapy after immersion in music and ceramics On meeting her husband who had also been in a cult On Adlerian psychology and its core tenant of belonging How making art reflects how we present ourselves in the world Coming to enjoy recovery work with those from high demand groups Getting involved with a somatic drumming group as a licensed therapist that turned out to be high demand When is it safe to explore art therapy after a high demand experience? How making art bypasses the language centres of the brain How to find an art therapist to work with Suggestions for using art on our own to heal Resources mentioned in this episode Article at the CBC website about art therapy for wildfire evacuees The International Cultic Studies Association (ICSA) The Lalich Center on Cults and Coercion The American Art Therapy Association The Canadian Art Therapy Association Julia Cameron and The Artist's Way Transcript of Interview with Natalee Bigger Stockdale Alexandra: Natalee Bigger Stockdale, welcome to Creative Alchemy. Natalee: Thank you, Alexandra. It's nice to be here. Alexandra: It's great to have you here. Tell us a little bit about your background. Natalee: Sure. I know we'll probably get into the professional part because that'll be part of art therapy. But for me personally, I grew up in Iowa in the U.S. So Midwestern girl, kind of rural and small town. I always loved art; was really drawn to that. But I was trained in classical music. That was my mom's dream for me and our family. And it was easy for me. Still worked, but I think the thing that was the easiest and just came out of me naturally as a maybe like a native language, if you will, or native expressive mode was through visual. When I was in high school, I had a really wonderful art teacher, and after I graduated, she told me art was always easy for you, and so that helped me define myself as an artistic person. Although I had all this classical training in music, and that's what I decided to pursue in college. Even though it's like a maybe a starving artist degree, I'm lucky that it ended up where I am. I've always followed my heart that way, and really value being led. I guess, like by my intrinsic interests. Let's see what else. I love being outside and out in the forest. That's always something that's drawn me back to myself is trying to get near, especially rivers. They just call me. Alexandra: You moved from undergraduate work into a greater interest in art therapy. How did that happen? Natalee: I moved from Iowa up to the Twin Cities for my undergrad degree. I focused mostly on painting and ceramics, and then I spent about seven years in production ceramics. And it is hard work. It's takes a toll on your body, my body, and there are a lot of different things. You don't talk a whole lot. It's a lot of numbers. I did glaze testing for a while, mixing dry chemicals. I did a lot of slip casting for my own work and dry clay mixing, so it was pretty. I don't know. I guess it was it was fun and playful at sometimes, but it's also this thing that turns into a job with deadlines and the hustle. And so, along with that, I would say in that realm, a lot of folks are there just for the art and production, not necessarily self-reflection and internal exploration. I was always longing for that and missing that when it wasn't happening in the production scene, and so I ended up moving.
